blocks.h: Each country answers the same five questions, from its National Adaptation Plan (NAP) where one exists, or from the best substitute source where it does not. Mozambique was done first and set the layout the other countries follow.

items: Climate hazards: what dangers the country faces, and where.
Actions under way: what is already being done.
Techniques in use, and where.
Most effective techniques: what the source says works, and on what evidence.
Future techniques: what the source plans or recommends.

blocks.h: Page references give the page number printed on the document, with the PDF page in brackets where they differ, e.g. p. 12 (PDF 24). French sources are summarised in English.
Confidence:
Five levels are used: High, Medium–High, Medium, Low–Medium and Low. Each answer has a short reason, shown on hover on the website.
Questions 1, 2, 3 and 5 (hazards, actions, techniques, future plans): confidence measures how clearly and specifically the source says it.

head: Level
Meaning for questions 1, 2, 3 and 5
rows: High
Stated directly and specifically in the source, with locations or figures
Medium–High
Stated specifically, but one step removed (for example a report summarising another study)
Medium
Stated in the source but in general terms, or pieced together from several passages
Low–Medium
Stated only in passing, or in a single secondary source
Low
Implied, out of date, or from a secondary source; check before relying on it

blocks.h: Question 4 (what works) uses a stricter rule: confidence measures how strong the evidence is that the technique works, not how clearly the source says so.

head: Level
Meaning for question 4
rows: High
An independent study that measured results, ideally against a comparison group
Medium–High
An independent evaluation that measured results but had no comparison group, or several independent sources that agree
Medium
A single study, a modelled estimate, or an independent review based mainly on interviews or delivery figures
Low–Medium
The project's, agency's or government's own report, with no independent check. This is the ceiling for any self-reported success
Low
Anecdote, a press report, or out-of-date evidence

blocks.h: A project's own admission that something failed or fell behind can be rated up to Medium, because it goes against the reporter's interest.

"Effective?" uses six labels: Yes (a measured result), Partly, Promising (early or self-reported signs), Not measured (delivered, but the effect was not measured), Too early and No. Any extra detail follows in brackets.

One list per question: official and outside sources are combined into one list of answers. Each answer names its sources, marked Official (NAP or government submission) or Other (evaluations, studies, World Bank and similar).

Each question ends with a Verdict on whether the official source is good enough on its own. Structure: each landscape opens with what applies across its borders, then its countries follow. Mozambique and Madagascar sit outside the landscapes.

10 of the original 14 countries have a NAP (Botswana's is only a process framework). Sources for Uganda and Rwanda are listed in their own sections. Angola, Namibia, Gabon and Republic of Congo have no NAP submitted to the UNFCCC, so each gets a substitute pair: its own government's adaptation submission plus the World Bank's Country Climate and Development Report (CCDR). The CCDRs are the only source type found that comments on which measures are worth prioritising.

blocks.h: Gaps that apply to every source so far:

items: Question 4 (most effective techniques) is the weakest everywhere. NAPs, NDCs and Adaptation Communications list planned measures but rarely evaluate them. Expect mostly Low or Medium confidence there unless we add evaluation literature, such as project end-of-term evaluations.
None of the four substitute sets is as detailed as a NAP. Namibia comes closest; Gabon is the thinnest.

side-note-techniques-used-elsewhere-in-e.title: Side note: techniques used elsewhere in East Africa

blocks.h: Source: Other WFP Regional Bureau for Eastern Africa, Climate and Resilience Actions in Eastern Africa (2023 results; WFP's own brochure, so figures are self-reported; printed page = PDF page). Most of what it describes is already in the doc for our countries (livestock insurance, savings groups, post-harvest storage, conservation agriculture, drought early action). Four approaches are not yet recorded in our areas:

items: Cash paid before floods, not only before droughts. In Somalia (2023), WFP's first flood early action in Africa sent warnings to 440,000 people and USD 2.7 million in cash to 218,000 people before El Niño floods, with boats pre-positioned on the Juba and Shabelle rivers. In Burundi, about 9,000 people received cash 3 days before heavy rain and 12 days before peak flooding (pp. 4–5). Possible fit: Zambezi and Barotse floodplains (Zambia, Namibia's Zambezi region), Kenya's Lower Tana, river floods in the Congo Basin. Mozambique has cyclone early action but no flood cash yet. Confidence: medium (self-reported, no comparison group).

Crop insurance bundled into a government input voucher scheme. In Amhara, Ethiopia, farmers are insured when they collect subsidised seed and fertiliser: 610,760 people covered in six districts, USD 1.2 million in premiums for USD 18.5 million of yield protection (p. 6). This tackles the low uptake that limited farmer insurance in Zimbabwe and Mozambique. Possible fit: Zambia's Farmer Input Support Programme, Zimbabwe's move to Area Yield Index Insurance. Confidence: low–medium (reach figures only, no outcome data).

Drought insurance where governments cannot insure (ARC Replica in conflict settings). In Sudan, WFP bought an African Risk Capacity "Replica" drought policy covering about 63,000 people despite the war (p. 7). Possible fit: CAR and DRC, where the doc records no insurance or risk finance at all. Confidence: low (policy bought; no payout reported).

Farmer Service Centres. In Kenya, 1,081 centres serve 244,008 smallholders (54% women) in drylands and high-potential areas, giving advice on storage and handling and linking farmers to buyers; farmers sold 6,377 t worth USD 3.7 million (p. 9). Possible fit: Kenya's SOKNOT counties and Tanzania's northern zone. Confidence: low–medium (counties not named; sales figures, no resilience outcomes).

blocks.h: From the wider literature (page numbers are PDF pages). Five more approaches not yet recorded in our areas:

items: Push-pull farming. Maize is intercropped with a pest-repelling legume (Desmodium) and bordered by a trap grass (Brachiaria); the "climate-smart" version uses drought-tolerant varieties of both. A study of 486 farmers (half adopters) in eight western Kenyan counties and Tarime and Rorya districts (Mara region, Tanzania) found adopters' gross margin from maize was about USD 439–474 per acre higher than that of matched non-adopters (Other Ouya et al. 2023, Agriculture & Food Security 12:15, PDF pp. 1–2, 5; peer-reviewed; matched comparison from one survey, no baseline). Possible fit: Tanzania's Mara region (SOKNOT), and Zambia's KAZA districts, where crop pests and disease were the most common shock (67% of households in the SCRALA baseline). Confidence: medium.

Ngitili dry-season fodder reserves (Shinyanga, Tanzania). A traditional Wasukuma practice: pasture and woodland are closed in the rains to keep fodder for the dry season, protected by village by-laws enforced by local guards (sungusungu). About 350,000–500,000 ha of woodland were restored between 1986 and 2001, helped by participatory extension from 1986 (Other Kamwenda 2002, Unasylva 211, PDF pp. 1–4; government forester's case study). A later valuation put a restored ngitili at about USD 14 per person per month, against average rural spending of USD 8.50 (Other EEA/TEEB case study, citing Monela et al. 2005; not yet seen in full). Possible fit: dry-season grazing reserves in SOKNOT and the KAZA rangelands. Confidence: medium (well documented, but the figures are about 20 years old).

Farmer-managed natural regeneration. Farmers protect and prune stumps and roots that regrow on their land instead of planting new trees. In World Vision projects, farm tree density rose from about 22 to 74 per hectare in Kenya and from 33 to 198 in Rwanda over three years, and participants in Kenya, Rwanda and Tanzania were 22–24 percentage points more likely than non-participants to report higher household income; Uganda was the exception (Other World Vision, FMNR Evidence of Impact, 2019, PDF pp. 7, 9, 11; the organisation's own evaluations, mostly respondents' perceptions). Possible fit: farmland around the Greater Virunga parks, and miombo farmland in Zambia and Zimbabwe. Confidence: low–medium.

Sand dams: a warning on siting. Concrete weirs across seasonal rivers trap sand that stores water. In Kitui County, Kenya, only about 42% of 116 masonry dams in the Tiva catchment met household demand through the dry season; most donor-provided dams in the county were not functioning; each costs at least about USD 5,000 (Other Ertsen & Ngugi 2021, Frontiers in Water 3, PDF pp. 5, 7; peer-reviewed review of field studies). Relevance: WWF's SOKNOT strategy plans sand dams, so siting and maintenance need care. Confidence: medium.

Safety-net public works that restore watersheds (Ethiopia's Productive Safety Net Programme). People in food-insecure areas are paid to rehabilitate watersheds and build small-scale irrigation. In study areas of Amhara, Oromia and Dire Dawa, households in supported districts had significantly smaller food gaps and higher resilience scores, but no better dietary diversity or calorie intake; resilience was linked more to water management on households' own plots than to public works on communal land (Other Balana et al. 2024, IFPRI Discussion Paper 2308, PDF pp. 3, 10, 19; mixed methods; the original random design was not fully kept, so these are associations). Possible fit: adding restoration and irrigation work to cash transfers in Kenya, Zambia and Mozambique. Confidence: medium.

blocks.h: Not yet checked: the Upper Tana–Nairobi Water Fund (downstream water users pay for upstream soil conservation), which could fit the Mara and the Okavango headwaters.

side-note-comparing-climate-vulnerabilit.title: Side note: comparing climate vulnerability across the landscapes

blocks.h: Source: Other WWF Africa Adaptation Hub with Anchor Environmental, Vulnerability of 263 Protected and Conserved Areas to Climate Change across Sub-Saharan Africa (factsheet, December 2023; assessments done 2018–2020 with the same method, to 2040–2060 under a high-emissions scenario; page = PDF page). It is the only source found that scores our landscapes on one scale. Scores are modelled biodiversity vulnerability for protected areas, not risk to people. Confidence: medium.

items: SOKNOT is the most vulnerable landscape. Mean vulnerability 23.2, against 19.3 for KAZA and 15.5 for TRIDOM. It also has the highest potential impact (35.7) and the most habitat change (pp. 3, 5).

By country: Kenya's protected areas are the most vulnerable of all countries assessed (27.3) and face the highest impact (39.4), followed by Tanzania (impact 36.1). Gabon's are the least vulnerable (13.6) and least affected (21.1), with Republic of Congo next (impact 23.5) (pp. 3, 5).

Capacity to adapt: Namibia's parks have the lowest capacity to adapt (46.1) and the least room to expand (26.9). Madagascar's are the highest (89.7), and TRIDOM's highest among the landscapes (82.7) (p. 4).

Species loss is highest in southern Africa, and in KAZA and TRIDOM among the landscapes (p. 3). Pressure from nearby communities is projected to be higher in SOKNOT (65.2) than in KAZA (54.3) or TRIDOM (41.6) (p. 3).
Only 4 of 263 areas came out "resilient"; 150 (57%) are "highly vulnerable" (p. 5).

blocks.h: CAR, DRC (outside the Virunga landscape), Mozambique and Angola outside KAZA were not assessed.

Method note: the "tourism demand" part of these WWF scores (same lead author) appears to use the approach in Coldrey & Turpie, "Potential impacts of changing climate on nature-based tourism: A case study of South Africa's national parks", Koedoe 62(1), 2020 (peer-reviewed). It links monthly park occupancy to mean monthly temperature; for South Africa's 19 parks it projects visitor numbers falling nearly 4% by 2050, mostly in Kruger (−6.4%) (p. 1). It looks at temperature only, not rain, water levels or wildlife, so it probably understates drought effects such as those seen at Victoria Falls. Its reference list points to two studies inside KAZA worth getting for Zimbabwe: Mushawemhuka, Rogerson & Saarinen (2018) on how tourism operators in Hwange National Park are adapting to climate change, and Dube & Nhamo (2019) on climate change and tourism on the Zimbabwean side of Victoria Falls.

side-note-nd-gain-country-index-2026.title: Side note: ND-GAIN Country Index 2026 (national scores)

blocks.h: Source: Other University of Notre Dame, ND-GAIN Country Index, 2026 release (data to 2024) and its Technical Report (page = PDF page). It is the only source that scores all 16 of our countries on one scale. The ND-GAIN score is readiness minus vulnerability, scaled 0–100; higher is better (p. 12). Vulnerability combines 36 indicators across six sectors (food, water, health, ecosystems, human habitat, infrastructure), each split into exposure, sensitivity and capacity to adapt; readiness combines 9 indicators of economic, governance and social conditions for using adaptation money well (pp. 6–7, 15–16). Ranks are out of 190 countries for the score and vulnerability (1 = most vulnerable) and 192 for readiness (1 = most ready). The quadrant uses the medians across all countries and years (pp. 13–14): red = more vulnerable and less ready than the median.

items: All 16 are in the bottom 45% of countries, from Botswana (#111) to CAR (#187). 14 are in the red quadrant; only Gabon (less vulnerable) and Rwanda (more ready, mainly because of governance and economic scores) are not.
Readiness, not exposure, pulls the scores down. 15 of the 16 are below the global median for readiness. This matches the doc's finding that plans are rarely funded or delivered.

Health is the most vulnerable sector in 9 countries, human habitat in 4, water in Botswana and Namibia, and food in Mozambique. Indicators that score worst across many of our countries are projected vector-borne disease, dependence on outside money for health services, low agricultural capacity (irrigation, fertiliser, machinery) and low dam storage.
Little change in ten years. Scores moved by no more than 2.4 points since 2014: Tanzania and Rwanda improved most (+2.4), while Zambia and Mozambique (−2.1) and Botswana (−1.6) slipped.

blocks.h: What it cannot tell us: the scores are national only, with nothing for provinces or landscapes. Exposure indicators are model projections, and the index deliberately leaves out actual disasters (p. 8). It measures conditions, not whether particular techniques work, so it gives context for Q1 and a baseline for comparing countries, but cannot answer Q2–Q4. Some inputs are old or filled in: disaster preparedness is self-reported and only covers 2014–2019 (p. 36), and economic readiness has the same value (0.247) for 19 countries since 2022, including Kenya, Zambia, Zimbabwe, Gabon, Mozambique and Uganda, so treat that component as unreliable. Infrastructure scores are missing for CAR and Rwanda. Confidence: high that the figures are read correctly; medium as a measure of real-world resilience.

The biggest remaining gap is Question 4: almost nowhere is there a measured result for people's resilience, and most of what exists is self-reported. The list below is ordered by how much each item would improve the analysis.

groups.title: KAZA landscape (Angola, Botswana, Namibia, Zambia, Zimbabwe)

intro.h: The Kavango-Zambezi Transfrontier Conservation Area (KAZA TFCA) was set up by the five governments in 2011. It holds Africa's largest savanna elephant population (about 227,900 in 2022, most of them in Botswana and Zimbabwe). Its hazards cross borders: water that falls on Angola's highlands feeds the Okavango Delta in Botswana, and the Zambezi links Zambia, Zimbabwe, Namibia and Botswana through Victoria Falls and Kariba.

Are national sources enough at landscape level? No. None of the national plans treats KAZA as a unit, and transboundary actions are either missing or only mentioned. The CAPA report is the only source found that reports adaptation results inside KAZA protected areas.

Other WWF Africa Climate Change Adaptation Initiative with Anchor Environmental, Climate Change Vulnerability and Adaptation Assessment for KAZA (4-page factsheet, © 2021, summarising Coldrey et al.; RCP 8.5 high-emissions scenario to 2050; page = PDF page). The full report was not available.

Official Bussière & Potgieter, KAZA Elephant Survey 2022, Volume I: Results and Technical Report (KAZA TFCA Secretariat, March 2023; printed page = PDF − 18). An aerial wildlife count over 60% of KAZA, with almost no climate content ("climate" appears once). Facts useful here: about 227,900 elephants, 58% of them in Botswana and 29% in Zimbabwe, crowded around permanent water (Okavango, Chobe–Linyanti–Kwando) and the artificial waterholes of Hwange (p. 104). Livestock were counted at about 736,000 head (73% cattle), roughly one domestic animal for every 1.16 wild ones (p. v). People and cattle are fragmenting wildlife habitat, worst in Namibia's Zambezi region (the Kwando and Zambezi–Chobe dispersal areas), which the authors say makes the ecosystem "less able to adapt to changing climatic conditions" (p. 107). A carcass ratio of 10.5% points to high elephant deaths, highest in Sebungwe (Zimbabwe), Angola and Botswana; fresh carcasses clustered along the Kwando–Linyanti–Chobe, and poaching was ruled out there (pp. 105–107), but causes are not given. Use: background on how dependent wildlife is on scarce water and where corridors are under pressure; a baseline for later surveys. It says nothing on adaptation actions. Confidence: high for the counts; low for any climate link.

(1) Other Steinberg (Chemonics), Livelihood-focused Climate Risk Assessment for KAZA (USAID Resilient Waters, December 2023; printed page = PDF − 8). The first landscape-wide, mapped climate analysis we have: 16 extreme-weather indicators from 16 regional climate models (moderate and high emissions, to 2050 and 2080), high-resolution flood maps, a community workshop (April 2023) and 20 or so recommended actions with timelines but no costs. It measures no results. (2) Official KAZA Secretariat, Livelihoods Diversification Strategy 2023–2033 (printed page = PDF + 1). Its climate section (pp. 31–33) summarises (1). (3) Official KAZA Elephant Action Plan 2025–2030 (printed page = PDF). One strategic approach (2.3) is "implement climate change adaptation measures". (4) Official Cuando River Basin Strategic Environmental Assessment (summary booklet, July 2025; Angola, Zambia, Namibia, Botswana; printed page = PDF). (5) Official Management Strategy for Forestry Conservation, KAZA TFCA 2024–2029 (dated April 2026). It does not mention climate; it covers fire management, illegal logging and the charcoal trade (objectives table, PDF p. 12). The KAZA Elephant Survey sent with these is the same file as before. Confidence: medium for (1) (models, clearly explained); medium for the plans in (2)–(5), which describe intentions, not delivery.

Other UNDP Botswana, management response to the terminal evaluation of the OKACOM project (UNDP/GEF support to the Permanent Okavango River Basin Water Commission; 3 October 2022; 11 pages, page = PDF page). This is management's reply to the evaluation's recommendations; the evaluation itself is listed below.

blocks.h: KAZA's main danger is multi-year drought, peaking in the 2023/24 El Niño, when Zambia, Zimbabwe and Namibia declared emergencies. Zambezi flows are falling: Kariba could not generate normally in 2022 and 2024, and flow over Victoria Falls fell to very low levels (sources differ on whether it "dried up"). Upstream, fires in Angola's peatlands threaten the Okavango's water supply. Wildlife die-offs at waterholes (Hwange, the Okavango Delta) show the stress on animals. Projections to 2050 add 3–4 times more days above 35 °C, a longer fire season, bigger river floods at hotspots such as Katima Mulilo, and less land suited to maize. Evidence on drought and river flow is strong; livelihood effects rest on fewer, smaller studies. A 2026 site-level risk profile adds local trends: rain fell about 59 mm per decade at Livingstone, while the Zimbabwe sites warmed fastest (0.19 °C per decade).

blocks.h: Cross-border action rests on the KAZA treaty (2011) and the river basin commissions (OKACOM for the Okavango, Zambezi cooperation). The main hands-on adaptation programme is CAPA, which works in six protected areas in Angola, Namibia, Zambia and Zimbabwe. Other efforts include a joint elephant survey (2022), human–wildlife conflict works (crocodile-proof fences, elephant walls around boreholes) and community fish reserves in Namibia's Zambezi region. New plans, such as the Livelihoods Diversification Strategy 2023–2033, the Elephant Action Plan 2025–2030 and the Cuando river assessment (keep it free-flowing), set direction but have no results yet.

works.title: Techniques with results at landscape level

blocks.h: Evidence is small-scale and mostly self-reported. The most promising result, though self-reported, comes from community river restoration: the flowing stretch of the Nsongwe near Livingstone grew from 300 m to 3.5 km. Other promising results are elephant restraining fences, which cut crop raids from about 80 a year to zero in one Zambian village, and conservation agriculture: in Binga and Hwange an independent evaluation found sorghum yields roughly tripled and incomes rose 22%, but children's diets did not improve. Artificial water for wildlife did not prevent mass deaths in extreme droughts. There is no landscape-wide evaluation, and KAZA admits its programmes rarely assess climate risk.

blocks.h: Verdict (landscape): the strongest landscape-level evidence is small and recent (community nature-based projects since about 2023, self-reported). There is no landscape-wide evaluation of drought or flood adaptation. KAZA's own 2006–2019 review admits that most programmes "have not explicitly assessed and mainstreamed climate risk" (p. 89) and that its impact monitoring system is not yet working (p. 60). The best evidence now is an independent evaluation from Binga and Hwange and KAZA's case study of elephant fences in Zambia. The 2023 USAID climate risk assessment now maps future drought, fire, flood and heat across the whole landscape and lists actions with timelines, but it measures no results either.

Recommendations converge on restoring rivers and wetlands with communities, protecting the Okavango headwaters from fire, and restoring wildlife corridors so animals can reach water in droughts. Others include diversifying tourism away from water-dependent attractions and replacing veterinary fences with commodity-based beef trade. On farms, the advice is conservation agriculture, water harvesting and small grains. For floods and fire: flood-smart zoning with forward-looking flood maps and a KAZA-wide fire programme. Climate information tailored to each livelihood and OKACOM's next phase (water allocation) complete the list. Almost none of this is costed at landscape level.

The OKACOM project's terminal evaluation (2022), now read, is the first such document found. An independent evaluation of the KAZA programme, if one exists, would be the other document to look for.

intro.h: Angola's KAZA area is the south-east: the former Cuando Cubango province (split in 2025 into Cuando and Cubango), with Luengue-Luiana and Mavinga national parks. It matters to the whole landscape because its peatlands and miombo woodlands are the headwaters ("water tower") of the Okavango and of Zambezi tributaries, which feed the Okavango Delta in Botswana. The country's worst droughts are further west, in Cunene, Huíla and Namibe, outside KAZA, and the sources say much more about those provinces than about Cuando Cubango.

Is the NAP good enough on its own? There is no NAP yet: a draft (PNAAC) is under national validation. The NDC 3.0 is the best official source and is unusually specific on the KAZA headwaters (fire in peatlands and miombo). Neither source describes adaptation projects in Cuando Cubango.

blocks.h: Angola's KAZA area is Cuando Cubango, the headwaters of the Okavango and Zambezi. Here the main recorded danger is late dry-season fire in peatlands and miombo woodland: 42.5% of the south-east's mapped peatland burned in 2023. Drought is the country's best-documented hazard, the worst in 40 years in the south, but it hits mostly Cunene, Huíla and Namibe, outside KAZA. It is projected to spread north and east. Temperatures may rise 1.2–3.2 °C by 2060, with rainfall swinging widely. Prolonged floods halted work in Luengue-Luiana National Park in 2025/26. Evidence specific to KAZA is thin.

blocks.h: Verdict (Q1): the NDC 3.0 is the only source that speaks to the KAZA part of Angola, and only on fire and water. Drought data are strong but mostly for provinces outside KAZA.

Angola is drafting a National Adaptation Plan. Most adaptation spending is in the drought-hit south-west, outside KAZA: the EU-funded FRESAN programme (water points, farmer field schools) and the Cuvelai Basin flood-warning project. National cash transfers (Kwenda) could be scaled up after shocks. Inside KAZA, a GEF/Conservation International project (USD 16 m, 2023–2032) is building climate resilience in Luengue-Luiana National Park, but it is slow: only USD 2.1 m was spent by 2026. Traditional early-season fire management is being scoped in Mavinga. Community river restoration on the Luengue River is covered on the KAZA page.

Few techniques are documented in Angola's KAZA area. Outside it, in Cunene, Huíla and Namibe, water points, farmer field schools and weather stations are in use under FRESAN. For the Okavango headwaters, the NDC proposes early dry-season (controlled) burning to replace damaging late fires in peatlands and miombo. This could avoid about 387,000 t of emissions a year in Cuando Cubango alone, but it is only a proposal. Desilting and protecting the Luengue River (on the KAZA page) is the one technique actually in use in the area.

blocks.h: There is no independent evaluation for Angola's KAZA area. The government admits that very few earlier NDC projects were fully carried out. In the 2015–16 drought, 80% of southern boreholes failed, and early warning is judged "subpar". The nearest evaluation, of the Cuvelai Basin project in Cunene, found that low-cost community measures were delivered, though their effect was not measured (water management, small irrigation, radio warnings). The equipment-based flood warning system and new drought-resistant seed, however, were not delivered in time. FRESAN built capacity, but hunger indicators remain "worrying".

blocks.h: Verdict (Q4): there is no independent evaluation for the KAZA part of Angola. A GEF project in Luengue-Luiana started in 2023 but had spent only USD 2.1 m of 16.15 m by 2026 and was rated Moderately Unsatisfactory. The nearest evaluation, for the Cuvelai Basin in Cunene (2021), found that low-cost community measures were delivered, but the equipment-based flood warning system and new seed varieties were not. The CAPA stories (Luengue River) show early, self-reported success for community desilting and protected water points; otherwise the main lesson is about delivery and upkeep, not techniques.

Angola's NDC 3.0 commits only USD 235 m to adaptation for 2025–2035, 0.06% of its NDC costs, split mainly between agriculture and fisheries (101 m) and water (44 m). Planned measures include forest-fire prevention, expanding conservation areas, water storage in drought areas, more weather and river stations, drought-tolerant seed, and drought contingency plans by river basin, including the Cubango. The World Bank suggests scaling up Kwenda cash transfers in droughts. Locally, conservation agriculture and fish farming around Calai are proposed. Little targets the Okavango headwaters beyond fire prevention, which is a gap for the whole landscape.

intro.h: Botswana's KAZA area is the north: Chobe District (Chobe National Park, Kasane, Kazungula) and Ngamiland (the Okavango Delta, Moremi, Maun). These are the wettest parts of a dry country, but they are among the most climate-affected and socially excluded districts. The Okavango Delta earns about 40% of national tourism revenue and depends on water flowing in from Angola.
Is the NAP good enough on its own? No. It doesn't answer any of the five questions. The CCDR is used as the main source, as for Angola, Namibia, Gabon and Republic of Congo.

Other World Bank Botswana CCDR (2025; printed page numbers; executive-summary pages in roman numerals); Lomeo et al., Science of the Total Environment (2024), via the Natural History Museum summary; peer-reviewed studies cited inside the CCDR; Lefebvre, *Terminal Evaluation of "Mainstreaming SLM in Rangeland Areas of Ngamiland District Landscapes"* (UNDP/GEF, draft dated 31 Aug 2019; printed page numbers) — "Ngamiland evaluation" below.

Official Government of Botswana, Botswana's 2nd Updated Nationally Determined Contribution (October 2024, English; printed page = PDF page). Fills Botswana's biggest gap: the NAP Framework has no measures, but this NDC lists 44 adaptation measures with baselines and targets (Annex 1, pp. 31–37), including wildlife corridors, water points in protected areas and fences, which matter for KAZA. It also gives a budget (adaptation USD 2.5 bn). Cautions: places are rarely named; many targets are "TBD"; and infrastructure was left out of the cost. Confidence: high that these are official plans; nothing is reported on results.

blocks.h: Botswana's KAZA area covers Chobe and Ngamiland (the Okavango Delta). These are wetter than the rest of the country, but they are among its most climate-affected and socially excluded districts. Floods are the most frequent disaster, and the Delta sub-district combines high flood risk with many poor households. Botswana depends on shared rivers for about 80% of its fresh water, so cuts in Okavango or Zambezi inflow are a major risk. The Delta's flooded area is projected to shrink 8% by the 2040s, cutting tourism revenue by 10–20%. In 2020 swings between dry and wet years killed over 300 elephants through toxic algae. Drought and heat are worst in the south.

blocks.h: Verdict (Q1): the CCDR gives a usable district-level picture. The NAP Framework adds nothing specific.

Little is under way specifically in Chobe and Ngamiland. The only documented project is the Ngamiland land-management project (UNDP/GEF, 2014–2019). It tested community fire management, conservation agriculture and planned grazing. Nationally, Botswana relies on drought relief, water-transfer schemes and basin cooperation through OKACOM. Community-based natural resource management runs in tourism areas around Maun, but residents feel the benefits go elsewhere. The NDC lists measures it says are under way, including the drought-tolerant Mosi cattle breed and conservation agriculture, without places. District climate committees were planned in 2020; their status is unknown.

blocks.h: Verdict (Q2): the only documented project in the KAZA districts is the Ngamiland land-management project (2014–2019), which was about land degradation but tested several drought- and fire-related techniques. Nothing current was found for Chobe.

Most techniques in Botswana's KAZA area are farmers' own coping: drought-resistant seed, shifted planting dates, water harvesting and reading natural weather signs. Credit shortages limit their spread. The Ngamiland project added two tested methods. Community fire management (Tsodilo Hills, Etsha) trained about 600 people, supplied fire-fighting kits and used mobile-phone warnings. Conservation agriculture, with subsidised ripping, was piloted with over 60 farmers. Planned grazing with herding and kraaling was also tried. Ecosystem-based adaptation is national policy, but only a principle so far.

blocks.h: Verdict (Q3): what exists is farmers' own coping. There is no programme-level record of techniques in the KAZA districts.

The Ngamiland evaluation (2019) is the only independent evidence. Community fire management worked best: burned area fell from 1.1 m ha (2014) to 0.2 m ha (2016) and fire outbreaks fell to zero by 2018, partly helped by drought. Conservation agriculture gave 2–3 times higher yields, but almost no harvest in the 2017–18 droughts, and it may not pay without subsidies. Planned grazing was barely adopted. Community trusts were the weak link. Tourism benefit-sharing wins little local support because residents see few benefits.

The Ngamiland evaluation (UNDP/GEF, 2019) is the only evaluation found for Botswana's KAZA area. It covers Haina Veld, the Tsodilo Hills enclave and Lake Ngami, at the western and southern edges of the Okavango Delta. The project was rated Satisfactory overall, effectiveness Moderately Satisfactory, sustainability Moderately Likely (p. 37). Most activities only started in 2017–18, so many results are early (p. 30).

The World Bank's CCDR is the main source. It recommends cutting water losses from leaking pipes (about USD 147 m) and reusing wastewater. It also proposes nature-based water security (wetland restoration, aquifer recharge) in the Okavango Delta and a careful look before any water transfers from the Chobe–Zambezi. Other priorities are diversifying tourism beyond water-based wildlife and cash transfers triggered automatically by drought or flood. The 2024 NDC budgets USD 2.5 bn for 44 adaptation measures. Its targets include keeping all protected areas, maintaining wildlife corridors, no new disease-control fences, and 70% of farmers using conservation agriculture. A full NAP is still to come.

intro.h: Namibia's KAZA area is the north-east: the Zambezi Region (the former Caprivi Strip, with Nkasa Rupara, Mudumu and Bwabwata national parks and many communal conservancies) and Kavango East along the Okavango River. Unlike the rest of Namibia, this is the wettest part of the country. Its main hazard is flooding from the Zambezi and Chobe, alongside drought and rising heat. Namibia has no NAP; one is being prepared.

Is the NAP good enough on its own? There is no NAP. The AdCom and NDC together are the best substitute of the four non-NAP countries: they name the Zambezi Region as the flood hot spot and list costed actions, some located (such as the Okavango riparian buffer). Neither reports results.

blocks.h: Namibia's KAZA area, Zambezi and Kavango East and West, is the most flood-exposed and among the most vulnerable part of the country. It has had 15 flood events since 1980, and rainfall here is expected to increase. The north-east warms fastest: +2 °C by mid-century and up to +4 °C by 2100. Drought is national and severe; the 2024 drought forced emergency measures, including culling 723 wild animals. Conservancies, covering about 59% of communal land, are "very vulnerable". Wildlife tourism could fall 15%, and wildfires and bush encroachment add pressure. Official evidence is good at regional level.

The flagship was CRAVE (GCF, 2017–2023, USD 10 m) in Zambezi and the Kavangos. It supported conservation agriculture, solar pumping, drip irrigation and a crop insurance pilot. Community conservancies and forests cover about 180,000 km² and are the base for most adaptation. Grants for ecosystem-based adaptation have gone to conservancies (FP024, SAP006). The NILALEG landscape project (closing 2026) works in the Zambezi and Kavango West landscapes. The government admits it has no consistent system to track progress, and some programmes stalled in 2025 when only part of the funds arrived.

Bush thinning on rangelands is a planned national priority.

blocks.h: The CRAVE final evaluation rated the project Satisfactory overall, but only 4 of 9 demonstration sites worked well. Individual and family farms adapted better than group schemes. Common failures were land disputes, poor contractor work and no maintenance after projects end ("once a project closes, there is no follow-up"). Conservation agriculture raised yields, but farmers can't sell legumes or afford inputs. The conservancy grants (FP024) worked: solar pumps and gardens were in use when evaluators visited Kavango. The SAP006 programme was rated Highly Unsatisfactory at mid-term.

blocks.h: Verdict (Q4): the CRAVE final evaluation is the best evidence for the KAZA part of Namibia, and it agrees with the government's own consultation findings: farming techniques can work, but markets, maintenance and land tenure decide whether they last. The final evaluation of the conservancy grants (FP024, 2023) points the same way: solar pumps and gardens worked in KAZA conservancies, but some contractor-built dams were poor.

Namibia's NDC 2023 is the most detailed plan in KAZA, with costs per action and USD 6.0 bn for 36 measures. KAZA-relevant items include restoring 5,000 ha of Okavango riverbanks (12 m), 5,000 km of firebreaks, wildlife translocation and diversifying conservancy livelihoods (113 m). It also plans multi-hazard early warning and upgrading flood-prone roads, plus fodder banks and adapted livestock breeds. The evaluations add practical lessons: build on what exists, settle land first, train people for maintenance, and ask communities to contribute.

intro.h: Zambia's KAZA area is the south-west: Western Province (Sesheke, Sioma, Shangombo, Mulobezi, Mwandi) and Southern Province (Kazungula, Livingstone), plus Kafue National Park. This is Agro-Ecological Region I and southern Region II, the country's most drought-prone zone. The 2023/24 El Niño drought, declared a national emergency, hit Western and Southern provinces among the worst.

Is the NAP good enough on its own? Partly. It is recent and its tables tag every hazard and action with provinces and agro-ecological regions, so Western and Southern provinces can be picked out. But it names no districts or parks, and reports no results.

Official Government of Zambia, Nationally Determined Contribution 3.0 (October 2025, English; printed page = PDF − 1). Much more useful than the NAP on targets and places. It names KAZA-area districts and sites for new work (Kazungula, Sesheke, the Barotse floodplain, Mosi-oa-Tunya), sets 2030 adaptation targets (Annex 2, pp. 36–37), and cites the still-unpublished 2025 World Bank CCDR. Cautions: there are no adaptation costs (they are left to a separate investment plan, p. 20); some targets contradict each other (flood-prone households protected: "50% by 2030, scaling to 75% by 2030", p. 21); and its 2007 flood figure (75 of 110 districts) differs from the NAP (41 of 72 districts), probably because the number of districts has grown. Confidence: high that these are official targets; low that they are funded.

blocks.h: Zambia's KAZA districts lie in Region I, the south and west, the most drought-prone part of the country. The 2023/24 drought, rated "one in 100 years", cut maize output by 54% and left 30% of people short of food. As Kariba fell, it caused power cuts of up to 17 hours a day. Temperatures are rising about 0.34 °C a decade. Floods hit the Zambezi floodplains in Western Province, and heat makes Livingstone's informal settlements up to 8 °C hotter. In parks, water stress, fires and human–wildlife conflict are rated high risk. Villagers in the Silowana Complex report livelihoods falling 38%, which they partly blame on wildlife damage.

blocks.h: Verdict (Q1): the NAP covers the hazards and places them in the right provinces, but not in the KAZA districts. Use the 2024 drought figures for current scale.

The main programme in the KAZA districts is SCRALA (GCF/UNDP), covering 16 districts including Sesheke, Kazungula, Sioma and Mulobezi. It supports climate-resilient farming, weather information, boreholes, goats, bees and crop storage centres. Just north of KAZA, the Barotse floodplain programme (USD 51 m) funded 2,233 community grants and canal repairs. For the 2024 drought, Zambia scaled up cash transfers to 1.63 m households and drew on catastrophe insurance. It is also adding solar power to reduce reliance on Kariba. The NAP names other projects, but mostly outside KAZA.

Conservation agriculture is the most widespread technique: SCRALA reached 154,296 farmers by 2022 (46% women) through 7,081 demonstration plots and field schools, including in Sesheke, Kazungula and Sioma. Weather stations and climate information reached about 234,600 farmers. Boreholes and small irrigation are in progress but behind schedule. Goat pass-on schemes and beekeeping run in Kazungula, Mulobezi and Sesheke, where honey output is high. In the Barotse floodplain, canal rehabilitation by cash-for-work, solar boreholes and fish ponds are in use. Water points and fire plans in parks are planned but not reported.

blocks.h: Verdict (Q3): the NAP lists techniques by hazard; only the evaluations say what is actually done in the KAZA districts.

The SCRALA mid-term evaluation (2022, "moderately satisfactory") is the best evidence. Conservation agriculture was widely adopted, but late inputs hurt yields. Irrigation fell far behind schedule, and goat disease killed many animals. On-farm trials show conservation agriculture and drought-tolerant maize pay off. In Barotse, locally led grants reached 581,028 people, and almost all households reported new income, though this is self-reported. Scaling up cash transfers "spared Zambians from the full impact" of the 2024 drought. Elephant restraining fences cut crop raids to zero in Kabula village. The SCRALA final evaluation is still to come.

blocks.h: Verdict (Q4): the best evidence is the SCRALA mid-term evaluation (rated "moderately satisfactory", ~66% of activities done by March 2022). The final evaluation, due after 2025, would be worth finding. The 2025 annual report (self-reported) says 84% of target beneficiaries were reached, but 2025 work was slowed by late donor funding.

The World Bank estimates USD 14.4 bn of climate finance is needed for 2026–2030; the NAP itself is not costed. Priorities include restoring the Zambezi Middle-Kariba catchment, which also keeps Victoria Falls flowing. They also include backing conservation agriculture with research and extension, and expanding irrigation to about 1 m ha by 2050 while managing the trade-off with hydropower. Others are scalable cash transfers (about USD 270 m a year), flood-proofing buildings and roads, and water points and corridors for wildlife. NDC 3.0 adds rainwater harvesting in Kazungula and climate-resilient tourism infrastructure at Mosi-oa-Tunya (Livingstone).

intro.h: Zimbabwe's KAZA area is the north-west of Matabeleland North: Hwange National Park (about 45,000 of the country's ~100,000 elephants), Victoria Falls, Hwange and Binga districts, and the Gwayi river area. This is the dry west (Natural Regions IV and V), where drought exposure is highest. Hwange has no perennial river and relies on pumped boreholes in the dry season.

Is the NAP good enough on its own? Partly. It is recent and good on national hazards, and names Matabeleland and Gwayi/Tsholotsho as hot spots. Its actions are sector-wide with no locations, and it reports no results.

A survey of 1,527 households in five wards of Binga District, between Chizarira National Park, Chete Safari Area and Lake Kariba; 668 (44%) had suffered elephant conflict (pp. 1608–1610). Households are very poor (about USD 6 per person per month) and 72% depend on farming (p. 1610). Living within about 30 minutes' walk of forest, near the protected areas, or near water points used by wildlife meant far more elephant visits, more crop guarding and lower tolerance; distance to forest mattered most (pp. 1611–1613). Households get no money from elephants, and the more mitigation methods they used, the lower their tolerance, which the authors read as frustration with methods that do not work (p. 1615). Recommended: early warning, chilli deterrents and beehive fences, buffer zones planned with communities, and community conservancies so that high-conflict wards earn something from wildlife (pp. 1614–1616). There is no climate analysis, but it shows why drying (more animals crowding at fewer water points) would raise conflict in Binga. Use: evidence for Q1 and Q4 on human–elephant conflict in north-west Zimbabwe. Confidence: medium–high for Binga (large random sample); low for elsewhere.

On adaptation it repeats the NAP (2024): the same 18 priority outputs and USD 10.31 bn cost for 2023–2030 (p. 8). New points: adaptation now covers seven sectors, and the government admits NDC 2.0 was off track. No places named beyond the national drought and flood maps (p. 7). Confidence: high that this is official; low added value.

blocks.h: Zimbabwe's KAZA area is Matabeleland North: Hwange, Victoria Falls and Binga on Lake Kariba. Drought is the main danger and is becoming more frequent, from about 10% of years before 1980 to about 25% since, with severe droughts in 2015–16, 2018–19 and 2023–24. In Hwange National Park, elephants died in large numbers in 2019 and 2023 as waterholes dried. Kariba fell to 13.6% usable storage in 2024, and Victoria Falls tourism drops after each drought. Chizarira has the highest climate vulnerability of all 27 KAZA parks. Heat stress is the biggest driver of economic loss, and floods now reach new areas.

Zimbabwe's main programme is Pfumvudza/Intwasa, national conservation agriculture on small plots with free inputs and over 5,000 extension workers. In Hwange, 110 solar boreholes pump water for wildlife. CAMPFIRE gives communities a share of wildlife income. A drought insurance pilot linked to Pfumvudza runs in four districts, including Nkayi in Matabeleland North. WFP runs anticipatory action and weather advice (PICSA), but outside KAZA. NDC 3.0 widens adaptation to seven sectors, adding tourism, forestry and biodiversity. Few projects are documented in Hwange or Victoria Falls.

blocks.h: The best evidence for KAZA is the independent evaluation of the FNI programme in Binga and Hwange (2014–2018). Sorghum yields rose from 93 to 324 kg/ha and household income rose 22%, but children's diets did not improve. In 2024, solar irrigation at Mlibizi (Binga) kept harvests going through the drought. Borehole water for wildlife did not prevent mass deaths in 2019 and 2023. Near Hwange, CAMPFIRE residents see few benefits. Elsewhere, WFP found that layering water assets, conservation farming and insurance gave the most reliable gains, but insurance gains faded in the next drought.

blocks.h: Verdict (Q4): the evidence for the KAZA districts is now better. An independent evaluation of the FNI programme in Binga and Hwange (2018) is the best evidence for KAZA: yields and incomes rose, but nutrition did not improve. A 2025 UNDP review adds one field observation from Mlibizi (Binga), where solar irrigation kept harvests going in the 2024 drought. Searching for evaluations of CAMPFIRE programmes in Hwange and Binga, and of GCF projects in western Zimbabwe, would be the next step.

WFP evaluation (2026): the independent evaluation of WFP's 2022–2026 plan supports layered packages (water assets, conservation farming, weather advice and savings groups) as the most reliable approach. It finds that weather-index insurance did not hold gains through the 2024 drought and that anticipatory action arrived too late in Hwange. WFP's 2025 resilience districts lie outside the KAZA area, so this is national rather than KAZA evidence (pp. vii–viii, 26–27).

Zimbabwe's NAP is fully costed: USD 10.31 bn for 2023–2030, including USD 1.39 bn for Matabeleland North. Agriculture (4.77 bn) and water (3.55 bn) take most of it. Priorities include drought-tolerant crops and livestock, climate insurance, water harvesting and groundwater, a denser weather-station network (150 m) and community conservation livelihoods (120 m). It also plans to climate-proof tourism infrastructure (210 m). The World Bank adds large-scale landscape restoration, with benefits above USD 400 m a year, and farmer-led irrigation from existing dams. The action list names nothing specific to Hwange or Victoria Falls.

intro.h: SOKNOT (Southern Kenya–Northern Tanzania) is a cross-border Maasai rangeland and wildlife landscape. It links Kenya's Narok and Kajiado counties (Maasai Mara, Amboseli) with Tanzania's Arusha region, Kilimanjaro and the Serengeti. Two cross-border systems hold it together: the Serengeti–Mara ecosystem, with the Mara River and the wildebeest migration, and the Amboseli–Kilimanjaro corridor (Kitenden). The same droughts hit herders and wildlife on both sides of the border.

Are national sources enough at landscape level? Partly. Unusually, both governments name the shared ecosystems: Tanzania's 2025 NAP has a transboundary chapter and proposes a formal Serengeti–Mara framework. But neither reports joint action or results.

sources.h: Sources: the Kenya and Tanzania sections; Other The Star (Kenya), "Mara River ails as Kenya, Tanzania fumble for cures", 19 Sept 2022; IFAW, Kitenden conservancy lease, June 2023.

Other WWF Kenya, WWF Tanzania, WWF-UK and WWF Germany, SOKNOT Transboundary Landscape Programme 'Unganisha' Refresh Strategy and Action Plan 2025–2030 (November 2024, endorsed December 2024; main-text printed page = PDF − 15). It is WWF's own strategy for the landscape: 160,194 km² in three sub-landscapes (Mara–Serengeti; Amboseli–West Kilimanjaro–Lake Natron; Tsavo–Mkomazi). It adds a breakdown of climate threats by sub-landscape, WWF's account of what it did in 2019–2025, and a costed action plan for 2025–2027 (USD 53.6 m). Cautions: the results are WWF's own figures, not independent evaluations; most 2019–2025 targets were never monitored for lack of funds (p. 10); and the climate projection map (p. 16) gives no numbers in the text. Confidence: medium for what is planned and where; low to medium for reported results.

two Mara River flow documents. (1) Official Ministry of Water, Lake Victoria Basin Water Board, Water Allocation Plan for the Mara River Catchment, Tanzania (March 2020; prepared with USAID's Sustainable Water Partnership, WWF and NELSAP; printed page = PDF − 10, front pages in roman numerals). It covers only the Tanzanian (lower) part of the basin, split into six sub-basins, and includes a climate-scenario model run with 20 projections to 2050. (2) Other Lake Victoria Basin Commission and WWF, Assessing Reserve Flows for the Mara River, Kenya and Tanzania (February 2010; printed page = PDF − 10). It is the joint scientific study that set the "reserve": the flow that must stay in the river for people's basic needs and the ecosystem, from the Mau Forest to the Serengeti–Mara. Cautions: the 2010 study uses 2007 field data. The 2020 plan says its three tributaries have no flow gauges, so shortfalls may be underestimated (p. 35). Neither shows whether the reserve is now kept. Confidence: medium to high for the analysis; nothing on results.

blocks.h: SOKNOT is rated the most climate-vulnerable of the landscapes WWF assessed. Severe drought in 2020–23 killed over 6,000 wild animals around Amboseli and 62,585 livestock in Simanjiro. The Mara River is getting shallower and more polluted, driven by forest loss in Kenya's Mau headwaters, farming and water abstraction; in droughts, flows already fall below the ecological reserve. Wildlife corridors are shrinking: the Kitenden corridor between Amboseli and Kilimanjaro has lost about 70% of its area. Warming is fastest in the drylands, and Kilimanjaro has lost 85% of its ice. Wetter wet seasons and drier dry seasons feed human–wildlife conflict and poaching.

blocks.h: Cross-border action is mostly agreements and plans. These include a 2015 Kenya–Tanzania memorandum on the Mara River, a joint reserve-flow assessment, and Tanzania's Water Allocation Plan for the Lower Mara (2020), which sets environmental flows for six sub-basins. Each country has its own wildlife adaptation or corridor strategy, but there is no joint SOKNOT plan. On the ground, a conservation lease keeps 26,000 acres of the Kitenden corridor open. WWF's Unganisha programme reports at least 6,644 km² of corridor habitat restored or under management. A southern Kenya consortium aims to raise new money, but that is not yet secured.

blocks.h: The priorities are a formal transboundary framework for the Serengeti–Mara with joint water allocation, restoring the Mau headwaters, and legally securing wildlife corridors with payments to landowners. Communities would gain from scaling up community rangeland management across the border. WWF's SOKNOT Strategy 2025–2030 adds water harvesting (pans, sand dams, protected springs), drought and flood early warning, grass seed banks and nature finance such as wildlife credits. It has a costed plan of USD 53.6 m for 2025–2027, not yet secured. A Mara water package of flow gauges and monitoring would put the reserve into practice.

intro.h: Kenya's main danger is drought in the arid and semi-arid lands (ASALs), which cover about 89% of the country. The 2020–2023 drought was the worst on record: about 2.5 million livestock died in 2022. Floods follow: around Lake Victoria, the Lower Tana, the coast, and increasingly Nairobi and Mombasa. Kenya has more independent evidence on what works than most countries here, especially for livestock insurance, cash transfers and community water projects.

Is the NAP good enough on its own? No. It is ten years old and has no indicators or baselines. The government's own 2022 review says it "was not able to accurately track progress" (review p. 27). Newer official documents fill most gaps; independent evaluations are needed for Q4.

blocks.h: Drought is Kenya's costliest hazard: the 2008–11 drought cost USD 12.1 bn, and the 2020–23 drought hit Kajiado and Amboseli hard, with above-normal livestock deaths and thousands of wild animals lost. The drylands, which cover 89% of the land, are warming fastest: Narok is up 1.75 °C. Floods strike every 3–4 years, mostly around Lake Victoria and the Tana, and in 2018 they also reached Narok and Kajiado. Climate already costs 3–5% of GDP a year, projected to rise to 6.5–8.5%. Mt Kenya's glaciers are almost gone. Evidence is strong and recent, especially in the 2024 Adaptation Communication. Outside SOKNOT, the AU's regional risk assessment links drought and pasture loss to local conflict in the pastoral north.

Kenya has one of the most developed adaptation systems in the region. Ending Drought Emergencies links monthly drought early warning to action in 23 dryland counties. County Climate Change Funds (now FLLoCA) give all 45 counties money for community-chosen projects. Livestock insurance covers eight dryland counties, crop insurance reached 1.5 m smallholders, and Hunger Safety Net cash transfers scale up in droughts. In SOKNOT, Kajiado has a climate-smart agriculture plan and is in the TWENDE rangeland project (83,706 ha restored), and Narok has a climate risk plan. A wildlife adaptation strategy (2022–2032) covers Amboseli and the Mara.

Techniques are well documented at county level. Index-based livestock insurance pays out by mobile money when satellites show pasture failing. Water harvesting (pans, sub-surface dams, rooftop tanks) added 1.13 m m³ of storage in 11 counties. Community-chosen water and rangeland projects run through county climate funds, and drought-tolerant varieties are widely released. Herders use rangeland management (grazing plans, reseeding, pasture field schools) and are switching livelihoods from cattle to camels, goats, bees and poultry. Drip irrigation, hermetic grain storage, cash transfers and mangrove nurseries are also in use. Human–wildlife conflict insurance is planned.

Independent evidence is strongest for insurance and cash transfers (both studied in the northern arid counties, outside SOKNOT). Insured herders were 27–36% less likely to skip meals or sell assets in a drought, if payouts came on time. Hunger Safety Net transfers raised food spending and livestock ownership, though gains were modest. County climate fund water projects worked at first, but many declined without maintenance budgets. Ending Drought Emergencies reports smaller livelihood losses in 2021–23 than in 2016/17, based on its own assessment. TWENDE found 49% of households now practise planned grazing. For crop insurance, new varieties and restoration, official documents report outputs, not results. Studies quoted in the AU's regional risk assessment find that pairing peacebuilding with water and pasture access helps herders through drought.

Only livestock insurance and cash transfers have rigorous independent evidence. Both work, but modestly, and insurance only when pay-outs are on time. The government's own review says Kenya "has had rather limited success" in raising smallholder output despite many programmes, and that the NAP cannot be properly evaluated (review p. 27).

Adaptation needs are estimated at about USD 38–44 bn to 2030, mostly from international sources. Kenya plans phase II of Ending Drought Emergencies (2023–2032) with drought early-action protocols. It will scale up locally led climate finance (FLLoCA) and extend livestock insurance to all dryland counties, bundled with credit and vet services. Cash transfers will expand. Other priorities are climate-smart agriculture, restoring degraded land and water storage with maintenance budgets. For SOKNOT, human–wildlife conflict insurance and climate-resilient tourism plans for parks such as Amboseli and the Mara matter most. The evidence suggests making insurance payouts faster.

intro.h: Tanzania's SOKNOT area is the north: Arusha region (Longido, Monduli, Ngorongoro/Loliondo), the western slopes of Kilimanjaro, and the Serengeti, with the neighbouring Tarangire–Manyara rangelands (Simanjiro) to the south. These are Maasai pastoral rangelands and wildlife corridors shared with Kenya (Amboseli–Kilimanjaro and Serengeti–Mara). The main hazards are drought and the conflict over grass and water that follows it.

Is the NAP good enough on its own? Partly. It is brand new and the most complete NAP in the study: costed programmes, a transboundary chapter and named northern ecosystems (Serengeti–Mara, Kilimanjaro, the Kitenden corridor). But its hazard evidence is mostly national or by sector, it describes no current projects in the north and reports no results.

blocks.h: Tanzania's SOKNOT area is the northern zone: Arusha, Kilimanjaro and Manyara, where drought is "a major problem". The 2021/22 drought killed 62,585 livestock in Simanjiro alone; the 2009 drought killed more than half the livestock in parts of the north. Wildlife corridors are shrinking: the Kitenden corridor has lost about 70% of its area, and changing rains push animals out of parks, raising human–wildlife conflict. Kilimanjaro has lost 85% of its ice, and its montane forests may lose half their habitat by 2085. Overgrazing degrades Arusha's rangelands. The worst river-flood risk lies near the Mara and Lake Victoria. Rain projections are highly uncertain. Outside SOKNOT, the south is projected to get drier and sea-level rise threatens Dar es Salaam.

blocks.h: Verdict (Q1): the NAP names the right northern hot spots, but its numbers are national. The 2021/22 drought losses show the scale on the ground. The World Bank CCDR adds the 2009 drought (more than half the livestock lost in parts of the north) and places the worst river-flood risk near the Mara River and Lake Victoria.

The most concrete work is integrated rangeland management led by NGOs in Monduli, Longido, Simanjiro and Babati. It covers grazing plans, dry-season reserves, village bylaws and clearing invasive plants. Joint village land-use planning protects shared grazing and water across village boundaries. Nationally, Tanzania has adopted strategies on human–wildlife conflict, elephants and corridor restoration. Pastoralists receive weather information by phone, and CRDB Bank lends for adaptation (TZS 107 bn). Larger GCF projects (Simiyu water, coastal marine areas) are outside SOKNOT. The NAP lists strategies without places or projects.

Tanzania's NAP is detailed and costed: USD 37 bn for 2025–2035. SOKNOT-relevant lines include sustainable rangeland and water management (1.2 bn) and mapping, restoring and legally protecting wildlife corridors (400 m). It also covers human–wildlife conflict measures such as fences, early warning and benefit-sharing (200 m), and community-led tourism (400 m). It calls for a formal Serengeti–Mara transboundary framework with Kenya. The World Bank adds joint livestock–wildlife land-use models with communal land certificates, private co-management of protected areas and livestock insurance. There is no plan specific to the north, and USD 12 bn of NDC funding is still to be raised.

groups.title: Congo Basin: TRIDOM and Sangha Tri-National (Cameroon, CAR, Gabon, Republic of Congo)

intro.h: The Congo Basin landscape here covers the rainforest belt shared by Cameroon, the Central African Republic, DR Congo, Gabon and the Republic of Congo. Three cross-border units matter most. The Sangha Trinational links south-east Cameroon, south-west CAR and northern Republic of Congo. TRIDOM links Cameroon, Gabon and Republic of Congo. The Cuvette Centrale peatlands span Republic of Congo and DRC. The Congo River and its tributaries (Ubangi, Sangha) tie them together, and their floods and low flows hit all five countries. Unlike KAZA and SOKNOT, no government document treats the Congo Basin as one adaptation landscape.

Are national sources enough at landscape level? No. The national documents mention the river commission (CICOS) and the forest commission (COMIFAC) only in passing, and none sets out joint adaptation goals. The evidence that exists is about forest carbon (REDD+, CAFI) rather than people's resilience.

All in French; summarised in English here.

Other Larrabure & Gardette, Mid-Term Review of the CAFI Fund (25 Dec 2020; independent; done remotely because of COVID; printed page = PDF page). This review covers the whole fund, not any one country, and it is about forest protection (REDD+) and how the fund is run. It hardly mentions adaptation: climate resilience appears only as one of seven themes in DRC's land-use plan (p. 49). Useful points: by 2020, 18 projects had been approved, 16 in DRC and 2 in Gabon. In RoC, calls for proposals were finished but no project had started. CAR and Cameroon were still at the policy-dialogue stage (pp. 9–10). Many projects were well behind schedule. Monitoring frameworks often lacked indicators, and the reviewers could not get a single project audit (p. 11). The review recommends opening implementation to international NGOs and adding activities aimed at women, young people and indigenous peoples (pp. 11–14). Use: background on why CAFI results came slowly. It is not the July 2025 evaluation of the RoC partnership, which is still missing. Confidence: high for what the review says about 2020; low for what it tells us now.

blocks.h: Across TRIDOM and the Sangha Trinational (Cameroon, Gabon, Republic of Congo, CAR), the rainforest's dry season is lengthening by about 6–10 days a decade. In a Gabonese park, forest fruiting fell 80% between 1986 and 2018, leaving elephants hungrier and more likely to raid crops, especially in the September–November rains. The Congo and Ubangi rivers swing between extremes, with near-record floods in January 2024. Forest loss remains high, and record high in Cameroon. Projections for TRIDOM show about +2.5 °C by mid-century and high species loss in all 12 protected areas, with Ngoyla the most vulnerable. Evidence on fruiting comes from one long-term site.

blocks.h: The biggest player is CAFI, which has mobilised over USD 1 bn for forest and land-use programmes. Results-based forest payments have started in Gabon and Republic of Congo. River commissions (CICOS) share hydrological data, though CAR's are poor. The Sangha Tri-national Trust Fund gives about €2 m a year to Lobéké, Dzanga-Sangha and Nouabalé-Ndoki. A cross-border TRIDOM master plan (2026) zones the landscape into core areas, buffers and corridors. Payments for environmental services began in 2025. Climate monitoring around the Dja reserve is due in 2026. Most of this is forest-focused, with little explicit adaptation.

blocks.h: The most-cited result, though mostly self-reported and contested, is electric and mobile fences against elephants. In Gabon a World Bank project raised farmers' monthly income by 40%, and the national programme reports 94% effectiveness, though that figure is self-reported. Community land-use plans and agroforestry are reported only in hectares. CAFI's own reviews show slow delivery: in Congo only 10 of 52 milestones were met.

blocks.h: Recommendations centre on an elephant-conflict package for TRIDOM and the Sangha Trinational: mobile fences, secure corridors and compensation or insurance. Others are shared flood forecasting on the Congo and Ubangi, agroforestry instead of slash-and-burn at the forest edge, and reduced-impact logging with community forest products. The landscape also needs new finance for keeping forests and peatlands intact. The TRIDOM plan adds a continuous no-take core area and a climate-smart land-use plan. Gabon's NDC budgets cross-border parks (about USD 75–80 m). Most of this is not costed for the landscape itself.

intro.h: The Central African Republic's (CAR's) part of the Congo Basin is the forested south-west: Sangha-Mbaéré (with the Dzanga-Sangha protected areas, CAR's share of the Sangha Trinational with Cameroon and Republic of Congo), Lobaye and Mambéré-Kadéï. This is the wettest part of the country (about 1,700 mm of rain a year and a rainy season of nine months or more). Most climate evidence for CAR is national, though, and much of it describes the drier north. Conflict since 2013 makes almost every adaptation problem worse.

Is the NAP good enough on its own? No. It is an "initial" NAP about planning. It says its own vulnerability studies were not updated and are "superficial, or even non-existent" for forests and health (pp. 64–65). It sets operational priorities only for agriculture, water and higher education (p. 76), and almost all budgets are "to be determined". It reports no results. Nothing in it is specific to the south-west forests. This is the weakest official evidence of the Congo Basin countries.

blocks.h: CAR's NAP covers national hazards, not its Congo Basin landscape, the south-west forests around Dzanga-Sangha. The best-documented danger is flooding, for example in Bangui in 2009 (14,500 homeless). Heat is rising about 0.35 °C a decade, fastest in the west, and the rains are becoming erratic, with dry spells inside the rainy season. Oubangui flows are down 19% since the 1970s. In the south-west, elephant crop raids and forest loss from farming (up 28% in 2025) are the main pressures. Monitoring is almost absent: only 3 of 13 weather stations work. The only local evidence on climate comes from the Cameroon side of the Sangha Trinational.

blocks.h: Verdict (Q1): the NAP covers the national hazards but nothing specific to the south-west forests. Flood figures are the strongest evidence. For the forest area itself, the only local evidence comes from the Cameroonian side of the Sangha Trinational.

Projects are listed with little detail and no results. In the south-west, the PDRSO project trains forest communes in community forest management. One small GEF grant (2021–22) supported agroforestry and beekeeping at Ngoulo and Lopo, on the edge of Dzanga-Sangha. Nationally, there is a UNDP farming and food-security programme (USD 44.7 m), a REDD+ strategy, a timber-legality agreement with the EU, and GCF support to prepare a full NAP. CAFI's first investment, a payments-for-environmental-services pilot, is near Bangui, not in the forests. Only 4 of 20 NDC measures were under way by 2021.

The NDC 3.0 puts adaptation needs at about USD 2.7 bn, with 64% for towns and infrastructure and only about 1% for forests and land. The NAP's priorities are almost all "to be determined". The one concrete, costed need is restoring the weather network (11 synoptic and 16 agro-weather stations, 100 rain gauges). Other plans include watershed management and water storage, short-cycle seeds and seasonal forecasts, transhumance corridors to prevent farmer–herder conflict, and urban drainage in 11 towns, including Berbérati and Mbaïki in the south-west. A cross-border resource pilot in Lobaye is the only forest-zone measure. A second NAP is promised.

blocks.h: Verdict (Q5): the official plans set out a process, not a programme, and cost almost nothing. The south-west forests, CAR's Congo Basin landscape, get no priority of their own. A second NAP is promised (NAP p. 72), and the CDN 3.0 cost table (now read, p. 52) puts 64% of the USD 2.66 bn adaptation cost into towns and infrastructure and only about 1% into forests and land.

intro.h: Cameroon's worst-hit areas are the Far North (drought and Logone–Chari river floods) and the coast around Douala (floods, erosion, sea-level rise). The number of people exposed to climate hazards each year rose from about 320,000 (2015) to about 3 million (2021). The 2015 NAP expired in 2020. A 2023 review for the environment ministry (MINEPDED) found that only 2 of its 20 projects were carried out in full, 11 in part and 7 not at all, and that results were never monitored. So there is very little evidence of what has worked. Since April 2025 the National Climate Plan is the umbrella plan for adaptation and mitigation.

Is the NAP good enough on its own? No. It is out of date and was barely funded: EUR 108 m for 2015–2020, against later estimates of over USD 30 bn. The two NDCs update hazards and plans but say almost nothing about results.

sources.h: Sources: Official PNACC (NAP, French, 24 June 2015); revised NDC (Sept 2021); NDC 3.0 (2025). Other World Bank Cameroon CCDR (2022, printed page numbers); project reports listed in Q4. Cameroon is part of the Congo Basin landscape; its southern forests sit in the cross-border TRIDOM forest area.

Other Planète Urgence, RACINE – Renforcer les Acteurs Communautaires Investis pour la Nature et l'Environnement (one-page project sheet, French, phase 1 2024–2027, funded only by AFD). Not the same project as the CAFI/GCF RACINE deforestation-free farming programme (2026–2035) in the Q5 table, despite the shared name. This one builds the capacity of local civil-society groups working on forest and biodiversity protection: 5 groups and 51 people supported since 2024, with the aim that 4 groups run restoration and conservation projects by 2027. No locations, budget or climate results are given. Use: minor; it shows support for local NGOs, which the 2020 CAFI review said was missing. Confidence: low (promotional sheet).

Official Green Climate Fund, Funding proposal package for FP311 – RACINE: Resilient Agriculture for Climate, Investment, Nature and Equity (GCF/B.46/02/Add.04, 28 Sept 2026; English; page = PDF page, the proposal section carries its own numbering). It contains the government's proposal (MINEPAT, with the cocoa and coffee fund FODECC), the GCF Secretariat's review and the independent Technical Advisory Panel's (iTAP) review. The GCF Board approved it on 27 Oct 2026 (GCF project page). Size: EUR 214.9 m over six years; GCF EUR 87 m (EUR 78.3 m loan at 0.75% over 20 years plus EUR 8.7 m grant), FODECC EUR 88.5 m, CAFI EUR 39.2 m in results-based payments (pp. 5–6, 111). The iTAP rated impact, paradigm shift, need and ownership high, sustainable development medium and efficiency medium to high, and recommended approval (pp. 111–124). Its main doubts: the project ties farmers further to cocoa and coffee just as the 2025/26 harvest fell (192,000 t to 125,000 t) and export earnings dropped 63% (p. 118); co-finance figures are only projections (pp. 122–123); middlemen may be pushed out of the supply chain (p. 119). The Secretariat rated MINEPAT's capacity medium, with weak procurement and audit practice (pp. 85–86), and FODECC's financial management needs strengthening (p. 107). Use: the main source for future adaptation in Cameroon's cocoa and coffee forest zone, and a good description of hazards there. Nothing has been delivered yet. Confidence: high for what is planned; low for results.

Official National Climate Plan (NCP, MINEPDED, April 2025, English; page numbers match the PDF). Other Tchindjang, M., Système de suivi, d'évaluation et d'apprentissage (SEA) de l'adaptation au Cameroun ("MEL review", MINEPDED with IISD / NAP Global Network, May 2023, French; printed page numbers). The MEL review is the closest thing available to a PNACC evaluation: it reviews how far the NAP was delivered and summarises the 2021 GWP formative evaluation (Tsama Njitat, 2022), which itself is still missing. It was written for the ministry by an outside consultant, so it is tagged Other.

Other Annual Report 2023 of the Sangha Tri-national Trust Fund (FTNS; printed page numbers; activity report written by the fund itself); CAFI, Annual Report 2025 (printed page numbers; written by CAFI itself; forest-loss figures from Global Forest Watch).

blocks.h: Cameroon's hazards differ sharply by zone. The Far North and North face drought, heat and desertification; about 2 m people live in drought-affected areas. The Logone floodplain saw about 400,000 people hit by floods in 2024. The coast, especially Douala, faces flooding, erosion and sea-level rise, and the Western Highlands and Adamawa face landslides. In the south and east forests, Cameroon's part of TRIDOM and the Sangha Trinational, the pressure is record forest loss: 125,000 ha of primary forest in 2025, driven by cocoa and oil palm. Heat and erratic rain threaten cocoa and coffee. Conflict in the Far North and anglophone regions worsens every risk.

blocks.h: Verdict (Q1): the NAP's zone-by-zone hazard picture still holds. Use the National Climate Plan (2025), NDC 3.0 and the World Bank report for current numbers and city- and department-level detail. The 2025 plan adds heat waves, drought risk to hydropower and a national vulnerability map.

The 2015 NAP was largely not delivered: of 20 projects, 2 were done, 11 partly and 7 not at all, and it was never monitored. The main completed work is the Far North flood-control project (USD 108 m), which upgraded the Logone dyke and Maga dam. Food-security early warning exists but is not linked to safety nets. Since 2024 Cameroon has set up new climate coordination and budget tagging; it is too early to judge. In the forest zone, a small sustainable-cocoa project near Lobéké (Moloundou, Salapoumbé) and the national cocoa and coffee subsidy desk are under way. CAFI had met only 3 of 33 milestones.

blocks.h: The World Bank notes that neither the NAP nor the NDCs are legally binding, and no law requires ministries to budget for climate change (CCDR p. 21). Stakeholders "rarely influence decision-making and implementation" (CCDR p. 24).

Verdict (Q2): neither the NAP nor the NDCs give a usable picture of what is happening. The project reports, the World Bank analysis and the 2023 MEL review are the main sources. The review confirms the NAP was largely not delivered. Since 2024 the government has set up new coordination and climate budget tagging under the National Climate Plan; it is too early to judge them.

The clearest programme-led techniques are in the Far North. They include the Logone flood dyke and Maga dam (completed 2018–19), controlled reflooding of the Waza–Logone floodplain (1990s) and rice-field levelling and irrigation on 7,500 ha. The NAP's annex lists farmers' own adaptations by zone: early seeds, shifted planting, off-season irrigation, hedgerows against dust storms and small dykes on clay soils. Mangrove restoration, climate-smart agriculture, protected-area patrols and climate-resilient schools are planned, not yet in place.

blocks.h: Verdict (Q3): the NAP's annex of farmers' own adaptations is valuable and specific by zone. For programme-led techniques, only the Far North flood works are clearly in place. The 2025 plan's techniques mostly repeat NDC 3.0 and World Bank targets.

Evidence is thin. The Far North flood plan worked in the 2019 floods (World Bank, self-reported), but some dykes collapsed in 2024. The Waza–Logone reflooding worked in the 1990s, almost doubling grass cover and waterbirds and largely ending herder–farmer conflict. The early warning system fails because warnings do not trigger support. Local climate plans have seen limited implementation. The NAP itself was mostly not delivered. Nothing has yet been measured in the forest zone; the new RACINE cocoa project has not started.

There is very little evidence for Cameroon. The NAP's planned annual reviews never took place. A 2021 formative evaluation (for GWP) was critical but has not been found. The 2023 MEL review that summarises it looks at how far the NAP was delivered, not at whether techniques worked.

blocks.h: Verdict (Q4): this still can't be answered properly for Cameroon. The 2023 MEL review answers a different question: the NAP was mostly not delivered and never monitored, so there are no NAP results to judge. The 2021 GWP evaluation (Tsama Njitat, 2022) is still worth requesting from MINEPDED or GWP-Cameroon, but it is described as focused on gender and implementation bottlenecks. For evidence on specific techniques, project evaluations (GEF, UNDP, World Bank, IFAD) are the better route.

NDC 3.0 is now the main plan: USD 33.8 bn for 24 actions (2026–2035), though about USD 9 bn of that is energy and industry. It includes resilient infrastructure and water (9.7 bn), health system adaptation (9.8 bn), climate-smart farming (2.5 bn) and forests and TRIDOM (0.87 bn). The World Bank recommends linking early warning to safety nets and making plans legally binding. The 2025 plan adds irrigation, fodder and livestock corridors, a climate role for municipalities and a monitoring system. For the forest zone, the RACINE project (EUR 215 m) will pay for deforestation-free cocoa and coffee.
