blocks.h: Verdict (Q5): NDC 3.0 is now the main plan and is much more ambitious than the expired NAP. Its "adaptation" total includes large energy and industry items. The World Bank adds governance fixes: binding plans, and linking warnings to support. The 2025 National Climate Plan sets targets by zone but no costs yet. Both it and the 2023 MEL review put monitoring and local government at the centre, the two weaknesses that held back the NAP.

intro.h: Almost all of Gabon is Congo Basin forest (88% forest cover, about 11% of the basin's rainforest). Close to a quarter of the country is protected, including Lopé and the Minkébé–Ivindo forests that form part of the cross-border TRIDOM area with Cameroon and Republic of Congo. More than 70% of people live on the coast, around Libreville and Port-Gentil. Gabon has no NAP yet. Its 2022 NDC says one is "being finalised" (p. 23), so this section relies on the NDC and the World Bank's 2025 CCDR.

Is the official source good enough on its own? No. The NDC is mainly about keeping Gabon a carbon sink. Its adaptation chapter is a two-page list of needs to be "quantified later" (pp. 23–24), with no places beyond Libreville and Port-Gentil and no costs. The CCDR supplies the hazards, the modelled losses and the only adaptation costs.

Official Government of Gabon, Troisième Contribution Déterminée au niveau National (CDN 3.0) (November 2025, French; printed page = PDF − 14, front pages in roman numerals). A big step up for Gabon. Unlike the 2nd NDC, which was about forests as a carbon sink, it puts adaptation first. It has a hazard profile with dates (pp. 6–7), four adaptation priorities, a sector table of vulnerabilities and options (pp. 26–28), a costed project list (Annex 4, pp. 74–85) and a budget (pp. 35–36). Cautions: most project costs were estimated during NDC preparation, marked with an asterisk, and the "disbursed to date" column is empty for every adaptation sector. The NAP is still being finalised (p. 26). Confidence: high that these are official plans; low that any are funded.

blocks.h: Gabon's best-documented climate impact is in its forests: in Lopé National Park, fruit production of 73 tree species fell 80% between 1986 and 2018 as temperatures rose. As a result, elephants are thinner and raid more crops, even near towns. This is unusually strong evidence of a change already happening. On the coast, sea-level rise threatens Port-Gentil, which may have to be moved, and parts of Libreville, where 37% of residents face flooding. Floods are the most frequent hazard nationally. Heat, drought and stress on hydropower are rising. Models disagree on the risk of large-scale forest damage.

blocks.h: Verdict (Q1): the NDC names the key threats (coast, elephants, migration), and the CCDR places them and puts numbers on them. The fruit-decline finding is unusually strong evidence of a climate impact on Congo Basin forest that is already happening.

Gabon protects its forests strongly: 13 national parks (11% of land), mandatory sustainable logging and a log-export ban. CAFI funds a land-use plan and forest monitoring, and a debt-for-nature swap (2023) pays for marine protection. Most of this work is forest and urban-drainage work funded for other reasons. In Libreville, AFD-funded flood and drainage works are under way. The measure aimed squarely at a climate impact is the national human–elephant coexistence programme (CAFI/WCS, USD 10 m, since 2025): mobile electric fences in all nine provinces. NDC 3.0 now makes adaptation the priority.

blocks.h: Verdict (Q2): more is happening than the NDC's adaptation chapter suggests, but most of it is forest and urban-drainage work funded for other reasons. Only the elephant fences are aimed squarely at a climate impact.

Electric and mobile fences around fields protect crops from elephants in villages near forests and parks, and are being scaled up. Reduced-impact logging (1–3 trees per hectare, directional felling) is used in concessions covering 60% of the country. Storm-drainage and watershed works are in use in greater Libreville. Dykes and sea walls exist on the coast but are not enough. Climate-smart farming (no-till, agroforestry, irrigation) is planned.

blocks.h: Verdict (Q4): electric fences are the one adaptation measure with results for Gabon: a 40% income gain in one project, and a reported 94% success rate at national scale in 2025. But the 2026 TRIDOM master plan calls Gabon's electric barriers "not sufficient" (p. 50), so the 94% figure needs an independent check. The forest record is strong but measured in carbon, not resilience.

Gabon has no NAP yet. NDC 3.0 budgets FCFA 669 bn (about USD 1.1–1.2 bn) for adaptation in 2025–2035, led by agriculture and energy. It includes five climate-resilient ecological corridors between parks, replanting six major river basins, and climate–health surveillance, but none is funded yet. The World Bank proposes a USD 450 m adaptation package: cooling for workplaces, flood-proofing and zoning in Libreville, and coastal protection. It also proposes USD 1.43 bn for water security. Other recommendations are to scale up mobile fences, secure elephant corridors and compensate elephant damage through insurance.

intro.h: The Republic of Congo's (RoC's) Congo Basin landscape is the forested north: Sangha and Likouala, with Nouabalé-Ndoki (part of the Sangha Trinational), Lac Télé and the world's largest tropical peatlands (about 5.5 million ha in the Cuvette Centrale). The south (Pool, Bouenza, Niari, Lékoumou), Brazzaville and Pointe-Noire face most of the floods, droughts and coastal risks. RoC has no NAP yet: the CCDR lists it among instruments still "being developed" in August 2023 (p. 67). This section therefore relies on the 2021 NDC, the December 2025 NDC 3.0 and the World Bank CCDR.

Is the official source good enough on its own? No. The NDC gives a costed adaptation budget and a long list of project ideas for GCF funding. But its hazard section is brief, and its table of adaptation actions (pp. 26–28) looks partly copied from another country's plan: it refers to "provinces", a "DNPM" department, an "NCCDMP" policy and "healthy islands", none of which are Congolese. Treat that table with caution. It gives no results.

This is the joint government–CAFI review of the 2019–2025 partnership, not the independent evaluation; it quotes that evaluation once (p. 24) but does not include it. It is about forests, land use and governance; adaptation is barely mentioned. Key points: USD 119.8 m mobilised (USD 55 m from CAFI plus USD 64.8 m co-finance, including USD 28.9 m from the GCF; p. 6), but only USD 22.3 m of the CAFI money had been transferred and about USD 9.7 m spent (p. 40). Ten of the 52 milestones are listed as met (Table 2, pp. 25–27), and all nine specific commitments are rated "delayed" (pp. 28–30). The partnership's governing bodies have not met since late 2023 (p. 27). A wood-energy project (PROREP) had its second payment withheld after an independent check found results insufficient (p. 36). The payments-for-environmental-services pilot paid 10 farmers by mobile money for 10 one-hectare agroforestry plots (p. 32). Use: the most recent picture of delivery in RoC, and some new detail for Cameroon (the RACINE project, pp. 44–45). Confidence: medium. It is a self-assessment and a draft, but it is frank about failures.

blocks.h: Floods make up 88% of recorded disasters, worst in Brazzaville, with eight major floods since 1985. In the forested north, Congo's part of the Sangha Trinational, the 2019–20 floods affected about 170,000 people in Sangha and 200,000 in Likouala. Low river levels and silting hurt river transport, and the Pointe-Noire coast faces erosion and saltwater intrusion. Heat could cut GDP sharply by 2050. Erratic rain affects the south. The northern peatlands, holding about 44 Gt CO₂e, overlap oil permits. The northern forests are covered more as a carbon asset than as a place where people need to adapt.

blocks.h: Verdict (Q1): floods are the best-documented hazard, in Brazzaville. The northern forests and peatlands are covered as a carbon asset more than as a place where people need to adapt.

Most action is forest-carbon work and studies. The Sangha-Likouala emissions programme (World Bank) supports reduced-impact logging and cocoa agroforestry, and land-use master plans exist for five departments, including Sangha and Likouala. Adapt'Action (AFD) supports climate governance and studies on Pointe-Noire's water and Brazzaville's stormwater. PREFOREST (GCF/FAO) has planted 466 ha of savannah agroforestry. A payments-for-environmental-services roadmap was validated in 2025. Agro-industry is steered onto savannah instead of forest. Few actions directly help people cope with floods or drought.

In Sangha and Likouala, reduced-impact logging and smallholder cocoa agroforestry are in use in and around concessions. intro.h: Salonga is Africa's largest rainforest national park, in the central Congo Basin, and WWF's only single-country priority in Africa. Its forest is almost untouched: 94% closed evergreen forest and 5% flooded forest, unchanged between 1992 and 2020 (Wallace Initiative report, p. 13). It was not part of the WWF 263-area assessment, but a 2024 park-specific climate report now exists.

The nearest evidence is in the DR Congo section above, which covers the central basin. The DRC NAP says heavy rain will intensify floods, landslides and erosion "especially in the central Congo Basin", as in the 2015–2016 floods that affected about 550,000 people and caused a cholera outbreak (p. 29). It also proposes a USD 95 m rural development programme for several provinces including Équateur (p. 60). Confidence: low, as none of this is specific to Salonga.

Other IUCN, World Heritage Outlook: Salonga National Park – 2025 Conservation Outlook Assessment (finalised 11 October 2025; 18 pages; page = PDF page). This is the independent assessment by the World Heritage Convention's advisory body that was listed as missing. It draws on the state's reports, a 2020 IUCN/UNESCO mission and the scientific literature. Overall outlook: "significant concern", with values improving. It is useful as an outside check on the 2024 state report, but it says little about climate. Some figures differ from the state report: it gives the management plan as 2019–2025 (the state report says 2016–2025), and donors as about 99% of the 2024 budget (the state report says about 94%). Confidence: medium to high.

blocks.h: Salonga, Africa's largest tropical forest park, is still largely intact, but drought has already more than doubled. Months of severe drought per 30 years rose from 21 to 48, and the longest drought from about 10 to 22 months. In 2024 a three-month drought hit community seed fields in the Monkoto corridor between the park's two blocks. Warming so far is small but projected to reach +1.7–2.2 °C at 2 °C of global warming, with 23–38% of species at risk of local extinction. More people are living in and around the park. Oil concessions overlapping the park remain the main non-climate threat.

The community seed fields were undercut by the 2024 drought, but every committee returned its seed, and 4 of 6 apiaries were colonised. Earlier alternative-livelihood work had no measured results; its lesson was that communities lose interest without concrete support, and isolation makes selling crops costly. Nothing yet measures adaptation itself.

blocks.h: Verdict: Salonga now has a modelled climate picture, which points mainly to more and longer droughts in a forest that is otherwise intact. The 2024 state-of-conservation report records a three-month drought that already hurt community farming in the Monkoto corridor. The park's community programme (seed fields, beekeeping, local hunting and fishing rules) is the nearest thing to adaptation, but it is not designed or measured as climate adaptation, and most results are self-reported. IUCN's independent 2025 assessment confirms better protection (large-scale poaching almost stopped) but rates the park's climate action "data deficient": nothing in its management is aimed at climate change.

intro.h: The DRC's share of the Congo Basin landscape is the central forest basin (the cuvette centrale): Équateur, Mai-Ndombe, Tshuapa, Tshopo and the neighbouring savannah–forest edge of the Plateaux and Kwilu. Kinshasa, downstream, takes the floods. The country holds about 47% of Africa's forests (128 million ha). Most of its climate evidence is national, and much of the data is old.

Is the NAP good enough on its own? Partly. It gives the national climate picture, a list of measures by hazard and a costed priority list (taken from the 2018 GCF country programme). But it relies on data from the 2015 Third National Communication, says risk assessments have been done only "on an ad hoc basis" (p. 29), and reports no results. Nothing in it is specific to the central forest basin.

blocks.h: DR Congo's NAP names the right hazards but gives little detail by place. In the central basin around Salonga, it says only that rain will increase and floods and erosion will worsen. Recent events show the scale: 2015–16 floods affected 550,000 people, Kinshasa floods in 2022 killed 169, and flash floods in Kalehe (2023) killed over 400. The south is drying and the rainy season is shortening. The Moanda coast is retreating 1–2 m a year. Warmer lakes threaten fisheries. Forest loss (1.28 m ha in 2025) is the third highest in the world. Without adaptation, GDP could be 5–13% lower by 2050.

Most action is forest and land-use work. A REDD+ pilot (2014) covered 12.3 m ha in Mai-Ndombe and Plateaux. The CAFI/World Bank Mai-Ndombe programme (2018–2024) produced 568 village land-use plans and 3,700 ha of agroforestry. CAFI's country programme has validated community land-use plans on about 10 m ha and 600,000 ha of new community forests. Earlier NAPA projects (2010–2015) improved weather monitoring and coastal work, and a guide (2019) helps provinces include adaptation. The sources show what was built, but not whether people became more resilient.

groups.title: Greater Virunga landscape (DR Congo, Uganda, Rwanda)

intro.h: The Greater Virunga Landscape is the Albertine Rift highlands where eastern DRC, south-west Uganda and north-west Rwanda meet: Virunga, Volcanoes, Mgahinga, Bwindi, Queen Elizabeth and Rwenzori national parks. It is mountain forest, lakes and densely farmed hills, not lowland rainforest.

Are the sources enough? No. Uganda's climate policy, agriculture NAP and 2022 NDC now give hazards and targets for the south-west and the Rwenzori, but no results; Rwanda's NDC 3.0 adds national hazards and costed targets, but names the volcanoes region only for its rainfall trend; and the DRC NAP speaks of "eastern DRC" and the Great Lakes only in general terms. The one evaluation covers districts next to the Ugandan parks (Kisoro, Kanungu, Rubirizi, Kabale, Rukungiri), not the parks themselves.

blocks.h: The Greater Virunga Landscape spans DR Congo, Uganda and Rwanda around the Virunga volcanoes, Bwindi and the Rwenzori. Its main climate danger is heavy rain on steep, crowded slopes, causing floods and landslides. Around Volcanoes National Park alone, 539 people were killed between 2013 and 2023. The Rwenzori glaciers have almost gone, and Uganda has been draining wetlands fast. Population density reaches 300–500 people per km² next to Bwindi and Mgahinga, and Rwanda's protected areas have lost about half their area in 40 years. In eastern DRC, conflict and crowding make every shock worse. The landscape's parks face the highest pressure from surrounding people of any WWF landscape. On the Ugandan side, rain fell by about 181 mm per decade in Kasese (1980–2015) and mudslides struck Kasese and Kisoro every year from 2021 to 2024.

blocks.h: Three large projects cover parts of the landscape. In Uganda, the wetlands project (GCF/UNDP, USD 46 m) works in Kisoro, Kanungu and Kabale. In Rwanda, the Volcanoes Community Resilience Project (World Bank, about USD 172 m, 2024–2028) combines flood works, early warning, terraces and a park expansion. Uganda's IFPA-CD invests in Bwindi, Mgahinga, Queen Elizabeth and the Rwenzori. In DR Congo, the Virunga Alliance links conservation with clean energy and jobs. Cross-border coordination runs through the Greater Virunga Transboundary Collaboration, set up by a 2015 treaty that is still not ratified.

blocks.h: No measured adaptation result exists for the landscape itself. Uganda's wetlands project was well behind schedule at mid-term. By 2025 it had restored 86% of its wetland target but only a third of the catchments, and many people still lacked other incomes. Rwanda's Volcanoes project is too early to judge. Cross-border coordination strengthened the secretariat, but DR Congo–Rwanda tensions blocked joint work. In Virunga NP, elephants rose 28% since 2020 despite the conflict, by the park's own report.

Volcanoes Community Resilience Project: early progress

In September 2024 the World Bank rated progress Satisfactory but every result indicator was still zero, 17% of the main credit had been paid out, and environmental and social risk was rated High (the park expansion moves households). By June 2025: 60 village land-use plans, 57 ha of terraces (71% of the year's target), 233 ha of trenches, 200 of 380 rainwater tanks, 11 of 15 river-level stations, but only 10 of 96 cows for poor households. The planned floodwalls on the Sebeya river were not approved by the Bank, so the first flood works moved to the Mugogo sub-catchment. Mid-term review due November 2026

blocks.h: Verdict: no measured adaptation result exists for the landscape itself. The only evaluation, from neighbouring Ugandan districts, showed a project well behind schedule at mid-term. By end-2025 it had restored most of its wetland target but only a third of the catchments, had given new livelihoods to fewer than half of the wetland users it moved off the land, and was under a GCF compliance action. Wetland restoration without timely alternative income looks fragile here. On the Rwandan side, the large Volcanoes Community Resilience Project has started building terraces and flood monitoring, but it is too early for results; its November 2026 mid-term review will be the first outside check.

The first landscape-wide plan to include climate is the Transboundary Strategic Plan 2024–2033 (USD 100 m over ten years). WWF recommends protecting climate refuges, restoring wildlife corridors and a joint cross-border climate strategy. Nationally, Rwanda's NDC 3.0 commits hazard-informed land-use plans in every district and large-scale terraces and agroforestry, within USD 7 bn. Uganda's NDC targets wetland and mountain restoration. The Uganda evaluation's lesson is to run restoration and new livelihoods together.

intro.h: Uganda's part of the Greater Virunga Landscape is the far south-west: Mgahinga Gorilla and Bwindi Impenetrable National Parks (Kisoro, Kanungu and Rubanda districts), Echuya forest, Queen Elizabeth National Park, and the Rwenzori Mountains and Semuliki (Kasese and Bundibugyo) on the DR Congo border. These highlands are among the most crowded rural areas in Africa, with 300–500 people per km² around Bwindi, Echuya and Mgahinga.

Is there a NAP? No full NAP; Uganda has three sector NAPs (agriculture 2018, health 2025, WASH 2026–2030). It began a full NAP in 2021 (NDC p. 13), but only the agriculture-sector NAP (2018) exists in our documents. The NDC 2022 is the main official source, as it has a full adaptation section with targets. Most rows are national; only a few sources name places in the landscape, so treat the national rows as background.

blocks.h: Uganda's part of the landscape, Kigezi (Kisoro, Kanungu, Rubanda) and the Rwenzori (Kasese, Bundibugyo), is mountainous and crowded. Landslides are the defining hazard: 90% of Kisoro's and 89% of Rubanda's people are exposed, among the highest rates in Uganda. Landslides killed 46 people in Kasese and Mbale in 2022. Floods in Kasese (River Nyamwamba, 2014) destroyed homes and irrigation and displaced people into crowded camps. The Rwenzori ice caps shrank 49% between 1987 and 2003 and may vanish by the 2040s. Erosion and wetland drainage degrade water supplies. Rising heat threatens Arabica coffee and brings more mosquitoes to the highlands.

Two named projects cover the landscape. The wetlands project (GCF/UNDP, 2017–2027) restores wetlands and catchments, builds small water works and weather services, and supports alternative livelihoods in Kisoro, Kanungu, Kabale, Rukungiri and Rubirizi. The World Bank's IFPA-CD is starting investments in Bwindi, Mgahinga, Queen Elizabeth and the Rwenzori: boundaries, trenches and fences against crop-raiding, and forest restoration. Uganda has three sector NAPs (agriculture 2018, health 2025, WASH 2026–2030) and began a full NAP in 2021. Catchment plans exist for 22 of 32 catchments.

blocks.h: Verdict (Q2): two named projects cover the landscape: the wetlands project (running since 2017) and the World Bank parks project (starting). National planning is advanced, but no district climate plans in the landscape are documented.

The one technique clearly in use in the landscape's districts is wetland restoration: removing crops from wetlands and marking boundaries, with alternative livelihoods. 55,132 ha had been restored by 2025. The same project built small water-retention facilities, fishponds and irrigation, and runs weather stations and early warnings for farmers. Trenches, buffalo walls and fences against crop-raiding wildlife, and natural forest regeneration in reserves such as Echuya, are planned under IFPA-CD. Nationally, rainwater harvesting, solar-powered water systems and climate-smart agriculture are spreading.

blocks.h: Verdict (Q3): wetland restoration is the one technique clearly in use in the landscape's districts. The rest is national or planned.

Evidence is weak. The wetlands project's independent mid-term evaluation (2021) found only 27% of wetland work and 16% of livelihood work delivered. Evaluators warned people would return to farm restored wetlands without other income. By 2025, 86% of the wetland target was restored, but only 34% of catchments. The whole year went on fixing safeguard failures after a GCF compliance mission. Early warnings reach farmers, but losses avoided are not measured. Cross-border cooperation has been held back by regional tensions. Outside the landscape, one study credits Karamoja's security-plus-livelihoods programme with ending most deadly cattle raids.

blocks.h: Verdict (Q4): weak. No technique in Uganda's part of the landscape has measured results on climate risk. The one evaluated project restored wetlands but struggled to give people other incomes, which is what keeps restored wetlands from being farmed again.

Uganda's NDC costs adaptation at USD 17.7 bn to 2030, 86% dependent on outside support. Targets include restoring 70,000 ha of wetlands, 10,000 ha of degraded mountain land, large areas of agroforestry and forest, and better forecasts and early warning. The WASH NAP (USD 276 m, 2026–2030) prioritises water storage, catchment protection and community early warning, which matters for landslide-exposed springs. The health NAP (UGX 240 bn) targets climate-resilient health facilities and disease surveillance. Plans specific to the landscape remain few; the evaluators' advice is to pair restoration with livelihoods.

intro.h: Rwanda's part of the Greater Virunga Landscape is Volcanoes National Park and the surrounding districts of the north-west (Musanze, Burera, Nyabihu, Rubavu), linked south through the Vunga corridor (Gakenke, Ngororero, Muhanga, part of Rutsiro). Gishwati-Mukura National Park lies further south along the Congo–Nile ridge. This is Rwanda's wettest, steepest and most landslide-prone region, home to about 2.3 million people.

Is there a NAP? A NAP Summary (2026) exists, but the detailed NAP and its funding plan are still to be written (Summary p. 55). The Summary adds hazards by district and a hazard-by-hazard list of actions; its project list repeats NDC 3.0's measures and costs (pp. 36–54). NDC 3.0 is Rwanda's most detailed adaptation plan: 23 measures with baselines, 2030 and 2035 targets, costs and lead agencies (Table 6.1, pp. 94–106), plus a section on loss and damage. It is strong on what is planned; evidence on results is limited to the government's own review and one project report.

blocks.h: Rwanda's part of the landscape, Volcanoes National Park and the north-west (Musanze, Burera, Nyabihu, Rubavu, and the Vunga corridor), is its wettest, steepest and most landslide-prone region. Between 2013 and 2023, floods, landslides and storms here killed 539 people, damaged 18,415 houses and destroyed 7,741 ha of crops. The May 2023 floods killed 131 people nationally, with recovery needs of USD 415 m. Rainy seasons are shorter but more intense, and the highlands will get more extreme rain. Soil erosion threatens over 1 m ha, worst in Ngororero, Muhanga and Gakenke. Food insecurity is highest in the west (31% of households).

blocks.h: Verdict (Q1): well answered. The Volcanoes area has official casualty and damage records by district, and the national loss-and-damage section is detailed.

The main project is the Volcanoes Community Resilience Project (World Bank, 2024–2028) across eight districts. It covers flood-control works, flood early warning (radar, weather stations, river gauges), catchment restoration, livelihoods and a Volcanoes NP expansion with a "smart green village" for 510 relocated households. Nationally, Rwanda has built 142,318 ha of bench terraces, over 1 m ha of progressive terraces and 525,000 ha of agroforestry, plus crop and livestock insurance. District disaster committees handle warnings, and a loss-recording system has run since 2016. A NAP Summary (2026) has been submitted.

Evidence is weak. Rwanda has invested heavily in terraces, agroforestry and early warning, but none of our documents measures how far they have cut erosion, flood losses or deaths. The project calls terraces "proven technologies" without data. The Volcanoes project is too early to judge: by mid-2025 terraces were at 71% of the year's target, and the first flood-wall design was rejected by the World Bank. The government's own review of NDC 2.0 found districts lacked skills and money and weak monitoring hindered impact assessment. A 2025 government household survey found vulnerability rose in all 30 districts since 2018, including the four Volcanoes districts.

Rwanda's NDC 3.0 is detailed and costed: USD 7.07 bn for adaptation in 2025–2035, 77% from outside. Targets include restoring 550,000 ha of erosion-prone land with terraces and agroforestry by 2030, and flood protection for 40% of high-risk households. Every district will have a hazard-informed land-use plan. A multi-hazard early warning system will link to every district, with 28 command posts. Climate-proofing at 7,325 schools is planned, along with agroforestry on over 1 m ha and payments for ecosystem services. Locally, the Volcanoes project still has to deliver its flood works in the Mugogo sub-catchment. A detailed NAP is still to come.

entities.name: South West Indian Ocean Seascape (Mozambique, Madagascar, Tanzania, Kenya, South Africa)

intro.h: This is the coastal and marine belt from Kenya to South Africa, including Madagascar. Hazards, actions and results for the coasts of Mozambique, Madagascar, Tanzania and Kenya are already in those countries' sections: cyclones, mangrove loss, coral bleaching, sea-level rise, and mangrove, drainage and early-warning work. This section adds the one programme that runs across the seascape, plus South Africa.

It is a desk synthesis of the nine sub-project mid-term reviews plus interviews with Blue Action Fund staff; there were no field visits, and the nine reviews are uneven, so projects could not be graded individually (p. 8). The SAEON page would not open, so I read the copy on the UNFCCC NAP site first through a text-extraction tool; the full PDF (identical to the UNFCCC copy) has since been read directly and all page numbers checked (printed page = PDF − 2). blocks.h: The South West Indian Ocean seascape runs along the coasts of Kenya, Tanzania, Mozambique, Madagascar and South Africa. Its main dangers are cyclones, which damaged mangrove nurseries and coral sites in 2025, and sea-level rise and storm surge in low-lying cities such as Dar es Salaam, Mombasa, Maputo and Beira, where "few, if any" are prepared. Coral bleaching has cost some reefs 50–90% of their cover since 1998. Mangroves are being lost, mostly to cutting and clearing, worst in Mozambique. Insecurity in northern Mozambique and political unrest slow coastal work. Much of the regional data is older (to about 2015).

blocks.h: The main regional programme is the Blue Action Fund's coastal ecosystem-based adaptation (GCF, about USD 63.5 m, 2022–2027). It funds nine NGO projects restoring mangroves, seagrass and coral and setting up co-managed marine areas in Madagascar (Barren Isles, south-west), Tanzania (Pemba Channel), Mozambique and South Africa (iSimangaliso). Tanzania declared two new marine protected areas, and Maputo National Park became a World Heritage Site. South Africa passed a Climate Change Act (2024) requiring provincial and municipal adaptation plans, and supports small-scale fishing cooperatives.

blocks.h: An independent interim evaluation (January 2026) rates the Blue Action Fund programme successful to moderately successful. It reached about 250,000 people and restored about 970 ha of mangrove and riverside forest. The clearest result is women's savings and credit groups, such as MKUBA in the Pemba Channel, which are likely to last. Mangrove and coral restoration gave mixed results. The biggest risk is the recurring cost of patrols, and some no-take zones may be too small. South Africa's national programmes report plans and reports, not reduced damage.

blocks.h: Verdict: the seascape programme reports good reach and restoration, and an independent interim evaluation (January 2026) rates it successful to moderately successful (2–3 on a 1–6 scale). The strongest results are in local governance, savings groups and women's empowerment. Restoration, new marine protected areas and early warning are well behind target, and no report yet shows less storm or erosion damage.

Recommendations come mainly from a 2015 regional report and a 2018 paper. They include coastal setback lines and building controls, building adaptation into integrated coastal management, and beach nourishment and dykes for low-lying cities, which models suggest would sharply cut the number of people flooded each year. A "green port" toolkit with eco-engineered flood protection is also proposed. Securing long-term finance for marine-area patrols and finance plans for new protected areas is the most urgent gap the evaluation identifies. None of these is costed.

intro.h: Mozambique's main dangers are cyclones and floods along the coast and in the central river basins, and drought in the south and in Tete. Its NAP plans 16 actions costed at USD 7.2 billion for 2022–2032, but says little about what has actually worked.
Is the NAP good enough on its own? Mostly for hazards and plans, partly for current action, and not for effectiveness.

blocks.h: Mozambique is among Africa's most climate-exposed countries. Tropical cyclones dominate: 21 hit between 1980 and 2019. Idai (2019) wrecked 90% of Beira, and Kenneth was the strongest ever to hit Africa. River floods strike the lower ends of shared basins (Limpopo, Zambezi, Búzi, Save); 8.5 m people were affected in 1980–2020. Drought caused 76% of disaster deaths, though sources disagree on which provinces are worst. Sea-level rise threatens a coast where over 60% of people live, and mangroves fell 18% in a decade. Rains start up to 45 days late, maize could fall 45% in Tete, and fires affect 40% of the country each year.

Mozambique has a strong planning system but weak funding. 135 Local Adaptation Plans were prepared, but few were carried out. LoCAL climate grants now reach 30 districts. The Beira drainage project (canals, retention basin, tidal gate) was completed in 2020, and early warning runs through about 1,500 local disaster committees. WFP runs resilience projects in 37 districts and Mozambique's first anticipatory-action framework for cyclones. A GCF/WFP project supports smallholder resilience in Tete. Coastal work includes the Blue Action Fund in Maputo National Park.

Well-documented techniques include green-grey urban drainage in Beira (canals, a tidal gate, and the Chiveve river restored with mangroves) and seawalls, which were damaged by Idai. Community radio, megaphones and local committees carry early warnings along the coast. In Tete, the R4 farming-risk package combines resilient farming, savings and insurance. Mangrove replanting through community nurseries works at Xai-Xai and Nhangau. Conservation agriculture, cyclone-resistant schools and health centres, simple home strengthening and mosquito nets and cholera vaccination are also in use. Solar pumps and drought-tolerant crops are planned.

Evidence is the strongest of any country in this review. Beira's drainage limited flooding during Idai, according to an IEG review and a post-disaster review (neither measured flooding with and without it), but seawalls were overtopped. Forecasts were accurate, but people didn't know what to do with warnings. Post-cyclone water and cholera response cut cases from about 400 to 4 a day. Anticipatory action for Cyclone Chido (2024) reached 114,000 people within days. Climate-smart farming with early action cut post-shock yield losses by up to 40%. Mangrove replanting succeeded where water flow was restored first. Local Adaptation Plans mostly failed for lack of funds.

Post-event reviews, based mainly on interviews, report that three measures helped during a real event: Beira's drainage, cyclone forecasting, and the post-Idai water and cholera response. Two work only in the right conditions: conservation agriculture and mangrove replanting. The GCF/WFP farming package shows only a small measurable difference so far. The NAP itself admits "poor quality of adaptation actions" (pp. 146–147). The 2025 WFP evaluation adds a fourth measure that helped in a real event, though its figures come from WFP's own monitoring: cyclone anticipatory action before Chido (pp. vii, 46).

The NAP costs climate resilience at USD 7.2 bn (2022–2032); the World Bank says USD 37.2 bn by 2030. The largest needs are water and sanitation (storage, small dams, dikes), renewable energy access and resilient agriculture (tolerant crops, conservation agriculture, solar irrigation). Priorities also include early warning that explains what a storm will do, mangrove and coastal protection in 21 coastal districts and stronger homes built with local materials. Funding Local Adaptation Plans is key, along with adaptive social protection and redesigned farm insurance. The full NDC 3.0 adaptation package is not yet published.
The NAP runs 16 actions in three phases: piloting 2022–24, scaling up 2025–30, then review after 2030 (pp. 182–189). The World Bank's estimate of the overall need is about five times the NAP's.

intro.h: Madagascar faces two different climate problems in two different places. The south and south-west (the "Grand Sud": Androy, Anosy and Atsimo Andrefana, home to about 3.7 million people) are hot, dry and very poor. About 91% of households there are poor, and repeated multi-year droughts cause hunger. The north and east coast (Diana, Sava, Analanjirofo, Atsinanana, Vatovavy Fitovinany) face the highest cyclone risk in Africa. Greater Antananarivo floods almost every year. Madagascar has a NAP (December 2021), the only one in this set written in French apart from CAR's. Madagascar is not part of any of the three landscapes.

Is the NAP good enough on its own? Partly. It is better than most NAPs in this set on hazards and places: it rates climate risk for each sector in each of the 23 regions (Table 4, pp. 22–23), and it costs and locates 12 national programmes (pp. 89–100). Its weaknesses are that it reports no results, its list of ongoing projects is a 2021 snapshot, and its costs (USD 273 m in total) are rough figures copied from similar foreign-funded projects. The national audit court later found the cost had been reassessed to USD 2.43 bn (2024). It also found that nothing achieved could be attributed to the NAP, because there is no NAP monitoring report. The full audit (October 2025) adds that regional risk assessments existed only for Boeny, Analamanga and DIANA, and that vulnerable and marginalised groups were not consulted (pp. 18–19, 31).

blocks.h: Madagascar faces different dangers in different regions. The Grand Sud (Androy, Anosy, Atsimo Andrefana) suffers drought and hunger: rain is under 400 mm a year, and the 2019–21 drought pushed child malnutrition above emergency levels. The north and east coasts take 3–4 cyclones a year; Cyclone Gezani (2026) affected over 600,000 people. Antananarivo and other cities face floods and landslides, with about 700,000 urban residents in high-risk zones. Rain is down 15–20% since 1961, and forest cover fell from 29% to 21% (2000–2020), worsening floods and erosion. Morondava has the fastest sea-level rise. The NAP's region-by-region risk table is the most detailed of any NAP here.

blocks.h: Verdict (Q1): the NAP's region-by-region risk table is the most detailed sub-national hazard data in any NAP here. (Its colour-coded risk levels don't survive in the text, so the exact rating for each region is uncertain.) The CCDR adds the numbers.

Much is happening, mostly through donor projects. In the Grand Sud, MIONJO (World Bank) stabilises dunes, plants green belts and builds water points. A new 28 km pipeline to Ambovombe opened in 2026. Cash transfers reached about 1.14 m households in 2024, and sovereign drought and cyclone insurance is in place. Antananarivo is rehabilitating about 30 km of drainage canals. On the south-west coast, community-managed marine areas and seasonal octopus closures run nationally. Over 1 m land certificates encourage tree planting. The government's own disaster system is thin, with only 3 of 16 planned regional offices open.

blocks.h: Verdict (Q2): much is happening, but mostly through donor projects. The government's own disaster system is thin: the national disaster agency has opened only 3 of 16 planned regional offices, and only one (Toamasina) works (CCDR p. 32).

Proven techniques are in use. Dune fixing, windbreaks and green belts protect fields in Androy and Anosy, and temporary octopus closures have run on the south-west coast since 2004. Cash transfers scale up after shocks in the Grand Sud and cyclone areas, and Antananarivo uses rice fields and ponds as flood storage. Madagascar has a full cyclone warning chain, the only one for any hazard, plus climate-and-health SMS alerts. Improved rice systems (SRI) and agroforestry are used locally. Drought-tolerant seed with index insurance is being piloted. Mangrove planting and sea walls are mostly planned.

blocks.h: Two results stand out, both from outside the NAP. Octopus closures raised catches at 36 sites by over 700% in the month after reopening, and village income more than doubled (peer-reviewed). FIAVOTA cash transfers gave beneficiaries 40% higher incomes and cut hunger compared with non-recipients. Insurance payouts reached all insured farmers, yet food security still fell sharply. Dune fixing and the Antananarivo drainage report outputs, not results: only 4.3 of 43 km of canals were done. The audit court questioned reforestation figures, and emergency malnutrition treatment saved most children treated.

blocks.h: Verdict (Q4): the NAP gives no evidence on what works. The two best results come from outside it: octopus closures on the south-west coast and cash transfers in the south. The audit court found that results could not be attributed to the NAP, because there is no NAP monitoring report.

The NAP has 12 programmes, first costed at about USD 273 m, then reassessed at USD 2.44 bn in 2024. The Grand Sud farming programme (719 m) is the largest, alongside the green belt against desertification, forest protection and climate refuges, resilient rice and climate-proof water. Coastal protection was cut to almost nothing. NDC 3.0 raises adaptation to USD 8 bn for 2025–2035, but only USD 50 m is unconditional. Its targets include 25,000 water points and a national register of disaster losses. The World Bank suggests funding adaptation by phasing out fuel subsidies.

blocks.h: Verdict (Q5): the NAP tells you what and where. The CCDR is better on how much, but most of its USD 7.49 bn goes to transport and energy, not to directly protecting people. The two documents agree on the main priorities: green belts in the south, climate-smart farming, cyclone warnings and safety nets. Neither costs coastal defences properly.
